Hon. CHARLES MURPHY (Postmaster General) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 246, to amend the Post Office Act.
He said: By an amendment to the Post Office Act in 1920 a new schedule of postal rates was applied to newspapers and periodicals. At that time the rate was one-quarter

of a cent per pound. The new schedule raised the rate on an ascending scale until it reached the maximum of 1| cents per pound, which went into effect January 1, 1922. Strong objection was made to this maximum rate, particularly on the part of publishers of small town dailies and of weekly newspapers circulating in the rural districts, and it was alleged that the increase represented an added expense of at least five hundred per cent to this class of publishers. They asked that the maximum rate be reduced to three-quarters of a cent per pound, or that in any event it be made not more than one cent a pound instead of the li cents established by the amendment of 1920. This request has been repeated at frequent intervals during the past year and a half both by individual representatives of these publishers and by delegations and correspondents, and after observing the operation of the act the Government is of opinion that the maximum postal rate on these publications might fairly be reduced to H cents a pound. It is to give effect to this decision that the present amendment is introduced.

subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN
speechtext:
That whereas the recent discovery of the insulin treatment for diabetes, by Dr. F. G. Banting of Toronto, as the result of devoted application and research, and the discoverer's disinterested and generous action in placing it at the disposal of the public, have conferred inestimable benefit, not only on the Canadian people but on sufferers in all parts of the world, it is expedient that Parliament should give some expression of the nation's gratitude to one who has rendered such distinguished service to science and humanity, and that such recognition should take the form of a vote of an annuity sufficient to permit Dr. Banting to devote his life to medical research.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary for me to supplement the words of the resolution by any comment; they speak for themselves. Moreover, the great service which Dr. Banting has rendered to science and to humanity is now known throughout the world. The government has felt that some formal expression by the parliament of Canada of the services of this distinguished Canadian would be fitting at this time and in giving it the form suggested by the resolution we believe we are interpreting the wishes of all Canadians. It is perhaps appropriate that I should recall that during the war Dr. Banting also rendered valuable services as a member of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and was wounded in action. We feel that in Dr. Banting, who was born in Canada and is a graduate of one of our own universities, Canada has a citizen of whom all who belong to the British Empire are justly proud. He has brought added fame to our country and in return, as the representatives of the Canadian people in parliament, we desire to express our country's appreciation of the great work that he has performed for science and humanity. We hope that by the provision which the resolution suggests Dr. Banting may be enabled to devote his life to medical research in a manner which will add to the benefits his discoveries in the field of medicine have already brought to his fellow men.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution, I think, constitutes a beginning, so far as public policy is concerned in this country, of recognition in any substantial way of scientific and humanitarian achievement. Dr. Banting being a Canadian and having achieved his fame and his contribution to scientific advancement in this country, it is appropriate that we as a nation should be the first to act in recognition of his services. I do not think, although not pretending to any particular scientific attainment, there can any longer be a doubt as to the supreme value of Dr. Banting's discovery and the beneficial, indeed the curative, pro-
Dr. F. G. Banting

perties which it possesses. Ample demonstration that this is the case has been made by those whose judgment ma3'- be taken as final not only in our own country but at various points in the United States and as well in other lands. What it means in the way of alleviation of suffering, in the way of contribution not only to the length but to the happiness of human life, it is impossible to estimate and quite impossible to exaggerate. That Dr. Banting should be especially rewarded and that at the same time the reward should take such form as would be to him an encouragement to pursue his scientific activities, seems to me axiomatic. I am personally aware- by those words I mean on the information of friends of his who undoubtedly know-that what this scientific man endured in the way of privation, in the way of personal sacrifice, in order that over a course of long years of experiment he might bring to fruition the objects he had in mind, is as yet, and probably always will be, unknown to the public at large. I can vouch for it that he made everything bend,-when I say everything I mean much that meant suffering to himself- he made all things subordinate to the attainment of his great goal; indeed, in doing so he only repeated what all men have had to do from the beginning of time to achieve any such wonderful result as he in this instance has brought about. Consequently it is only just to the people of our country, only just to the good name of Canada that this parliament should in a fitting way recognize what he has done for the nation and for the world. It is best from the standpoint of interest that we do it; for it will enable Dr. Banting from now on to pursue investigations along similar and other lines, from which investigations there is at least reasonable hope that results will ensue of great benefit to the human race. Therefore, as one who feels that the country should act in honour to its citizens; as one who feels as well that the greatest benefits to the world in the future are to come from scientific research and scientific achievement,
I have real pleasure in seconding the resolution.

subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel very happy to have the privilege of being associated with the resolution now before the House. Dr. Banting's name is now known all over the world, and it is peculiarly gratifying to the Canadian people that a discovery so important and of such great benefit to humanity should have been made by a Canadian. I feel sure that money will have no peculiar attraction for Dr. Banting ; that his great ambition is to achieve some-
thing for the benefit and the service of humanity. However, I am very glad that we are making some contribution which will in effect be opening the door of opportunity to him so that he can more consistently devote his time to the great work he has undertaken, a work which is a blessing to humanity and the results accruing from which bring honour to himself as well as to his country. I repeat that I am pleased to be associated with hon. members of the House in paying this tribute to Dr. Banting,-a man whom the people delight to honour.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister in charge of the Department of Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to add just a few words in support of the resolution introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and to unite with him, the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), in paying tribute to the eminent physician who has achieved so much in the path of science, and particularly of medicine, in Canada. This move of the House of Commons will redound not only to its own credit, but, I submit, to the credit of Canada as a whole. It is a sincere though feeble endeavour to recognize the services of one who through many long days and nights has devoted his efforts unremittingly to forwarding the cause of science, and who has, as it were, drawn aside the curtain which hides from the human eye some of the numberless mysteries of science. The exact nature of Dr. Banting's discovery is still obscure to the layman. In a word, it consists in reducing or controlling pathological activities which are normal in the human body if not carried to exaggeration. Sugar is an element of nutrition, important-indeed, essential-to the life of man but if it is produced in exaggerated quantities the result is disaster to the human body. The , discovery of Dr. Banting tends to check this exaggerated fabrication of sugar in the system, and it is hoped that the use of insulin will not only temporarily reduce that pathological activity but do away with it entirely. Canada is still a young nation. It has however in the spheres of industry, agriculture and commerce accomplished enormous results. Unlike the European countries its steps have been somewhat slow in the field of science, literature and the fine arts. Only a few months ago it was my inestimable privilege to preside at the opening of an exhibition of paintings in our Museum. Those paintings were exclusively the work of Canadians, and I cannot say how much impressed I was by the excellence of the exhibits. Time will come, and only time can

Dr. F. G. Banting
accomplish that, when Canada will take her place among the older European nations in the field of fine arts, sculpture, music and painting. Dr. Banting's discovery does not *ank as an achievement in the fine arts. It is a good deal more than that and will bring its own special advantages to humanity at large. And so I say it is the duty of the Parliament of Canada to take whatever steps are calculated to encourage men to devote *their time with enthusiasm to scientific research, especially when the results of that work are to help humanity and relieve its sufferings.
Mr. Speaker, I think this House will accept the resolution unanimously, and as the minister presiding over the Department of Health I wish to say in the name of Canada that we extend our hearty congratulations and encouragement to this young physician, who has become illustrious not only in this country but in the world at large.

subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN
speechtext: When this question was before the House on the 27th of February last the minister took the position that he could not do anything for Dr. Banting. I notice that the resolution does not include the name of Mr. C. H. Best, Dr. Banting's co-worker and associate. I think the country will approve the action of this Government in granting this annuity to Dr. Banting. It is a step in the right direction to recognize these men who are Canadians and Britishers for contributing something towards the advancement of medical science. It is well they should receive some recognition before they have died or left the countiy. I should like to find out from the minister if the name of Mr. Best is going to be included, and if any recognition is to be given to Dr. Macallum, who has made important discoveries in helium, and to other Canadian scientists. The Government of the Province of Ontario has appropriated $10,000 per year to establish a chair in the University of Toronto for continuing Dr. Banting's work. I think something might be done as well for Mr. Best, Dr. Banting's associate and coworker.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN
speechtext:
I should just like to point out one fact in connection with this grant by the parliament of Canada to Dr. Banting which has not been mentioned, and that is the fact as I am informed on very good authority, that Dr. Banting could have exploited this discovery and was offered an almost fabulous sum for the purpose of exploiting the remedy which he has discovered. If
you look down through the history of medicine you will find, with one exception I think, that every discovery that has been made by a medical man in an effort to cure disease has been given freely to the world. Take antisepsis, which was discovered by Lord Lister, anaesthesia by Simpson and Morton, vaccination by Jenner, three of the most outstanding discoveries in scientific medicine in the history of the world and without which much of the health of to-day would be impossible. All these discoveries were given to the world freely. It might be of interest to the House, and I do not wish to utter any word of ill-feeling against anyone in this connection, to know that the one exception that occurs to my mind where a medical discovery was exploited was the preparation 606 which was discovered by Erlich, of Berlin, Germany. I personally am particularly glad, as I am sure is every medical man in the House, to see Canada taking this attitude towards the discoverer of a health-giving remedy, for unfortunately in the history of medicine and surgery too seldom has recognition been given. There is one country in the world, however, which has on many occasions honoured its scientific men more perhaps than any other country, and that is the Republic of France. As you walk around the streets of Paris you will frequently come upon a street named after some distinguished scientist, the Avenue Pasteur, for instance, and you will find many statues and monuments commemorating the men who have shown great learning in scientific work. I wish as a medical man, like the Minister of Health himself, to congratulate the government and parliament upon having decided to do this worthy thing.

subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN
speechtext:
As we in this corner of the House have so frequently criticised public expenditure it is a great pleasure to be able to recognize the justice of the principles underlying this grant. I am not quite sure that it is setting a very good precedent for parliament to make grants in special cases, since I presume this body is hardly in a position to decide exactly v'ho most merits recognition of this character, but until we have some other body constituted for the purpose I am very glad to see that we are recognizing an achievement of this character. I take it from the remarks which have been made in this House and throughout the country generally that there has been a real contribution in this case and that we are proceeding along right lines when we recognize advances that are made in the scientific world. This action appeals, too, because in this particular case the achievement is one that is made

Dr. F. G. Banting

in the interests of the saving of life, whereas very often we have honoured as our greatest heroes those who have made their achievements not in the saving but in the destruction of life. It is a decided advance when we begin to understand that the saving of life is infinitely greater than the destruction of life for any purpose whatever.
There is another point to which I would call attention, and that is that we are getting away from the idea that men will accomplish great things simply to attain monetary success and only under the spur of competition. These motives have been held before us as the only ones which control men's activities at the present time, and I am glad to think that we recognize that men can work and work hard for other than financial advantage.
I like the way in which the motion is expressed, that this grant is made not only as a material recognition of past work but in order that this scientist may be able to continue to carry on his work. We have had the statement put forth very frequently that unless men were driven by the necessity of achieving some financial success they would not do any work. I believe that idea is absolutely wrong. If they are at all assured that they will have a competency, the truest men will go forward to accomplish even greater results. This recognition is probably an act of justice in one case; but we must look forward to planning that a great many of the more obscure workers in the fields of industrial and scientific research, as well as in many other departments of our life to-day, shall be given the same opportunity which has been accorded to this one scientific student-that is the opportunity of carrying forward their work and of performing something worth while in the service of humanity.

subtopic: DR. F. G. BANTING EXPRESSION OF THE NATION'S GRATITUDE TO THE DISCOVERER OF INSULIN
speechtext: On behalf of the University of Toronto, and the other universities of Canada, I desire to thank parliament for this recognition of the discovery made by a worthy son of a Canadian college, Dr. Banting. Undoubtedly this action by parliament will have a beneficial influence within the University of Toronto, and the other universities of the country, and encourage their graduates, professors and students in the service of humanity and progress.
Motion agreed to.

As I mentioned to the

It was pointed out in their communication to our government that any legislation on this subject by the Canadian government might be misunderstood in Japan, particularly if it appeared to be of the nature of exclusion; the Japanese government, it was stated, were anxious, on the one hand, to avoid any unrest in their own country, and, on the other to further the wishes of the Canadian parliament in a friendly way. At the request of many Toronto organizations, including the mayor and the corporation of the city, I desire to bring before the House this morning and discuss for about ten minutes the case of the city of Toronto and its agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway and its successors and assigns, now the government of Canada, and the Canadian Pacific Railway for the erection of a viaduct across the waterfront in Toronto. The lower end of the city of Toronto on Front street, between Yonge and York, resembles a city or town in Flanders or France, destroyed in the late war by the German government. The city of Toronto placed a contract with the railways before the Railway Commission, and after ten years of effort before that body, the othei day a meeting was held at the City Hall in Toronto, at which meeting the Railway Board washed its hands of the whole agreement, and the matter is now in the hands of the government to decide. The statement of the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners delivered at the City Hall, Toronto, on Thursday the 7th June last, was as follows:
This board has nothing to say as to whether the viaduct scheme will go through or not. It is out of our hands. We went so far as to say in Ottawa in 1921 that we would not interfere. It is now a matter for those concerned to raise the money.
The government is a party to the contract. The parties to the contract were the corporation of the city of Toronto, the Toronto Harbour Commissioners, and the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada;-it is now the Grand Trunk Railway and their successors and assigns, who are now the government. The city of Toronto has been treated in a most unjust and unfair way, not onljr by the present government, but by the preceding governments, in failing to carry out this agreement. The disgraceful conditions in Toronto have made that city waterfront a by-word for more than twenty years. Behind the presidents of the

railways, whose policy has been a compound of evasion and procrastination, is the Railway Commission, the members of which washed their hands of the case, after loudly declaring that final jurisdiction rested with them. The Railway Commission is supposed to enforce the agreement between the municipalities and the railways and they have washed their hands of the affair. A large revenue has been contributed by the city towards the National Railways. The only forum we can go to and ask for the enforcement of this agreement is the parliament of Canada. An agreement is an agreement in law, even if it is made by a municipal corporation and the Grand Trunk. The government can be brought into the Exchequer Court and adjudicated in that way. Matters have been.allowed to drift along till the present time. We have a station there which the Grand Trunk built some ten years ago, and it is now ready to be opened. But that station is an eyesore to everybody coming into the city. It is an up-to-date station, made to fit in with the elevated tracks which were proposed to be constructed. When this agreement was entered into the Harbour Commissioners did not look upon it as "a scrap of paper," but considered it a binding agreement between the railways and the city. They laid their plans before the government for the rebuilding of the harbour at Toronto at a cost of 826,000,000. Now,
820,000,000 of that money have been expended to-day to provide a right of way for this viaduct, and to provide new piers and breakwaters, for the carrying out of the agreement. Why is this document treated as a scrap of paper? Can the railways of this country ride rough-shod over municipalities of Canada in this way, and treat a solemn agreement as a scrap of paper? An agreement is an agreement no matter by whom it is made; and we say that Canada is a party to it, because under the description in the agreement the party of the second part is the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada hereinafter called the railway company and their successors and assigns. They are bound by that agreement. The Grand Trunk is not bankrupt. The sum of $73,000,000 was voted by this government the other night for railways and $26,000,000 in addition was for the purpose of extensions and branch lines. Many of these lines, of course, are not revenue producing, but for many years the branch lines have been producing a revenue. The Grand Trunk made most of its money in Ontario, and if the Grand Trunk had not been made a link in the Canadian National Railways they would have made money. According to the Acworth Report

Supply-Toronto Viaduct
on Railways of 1917 there was taken, out of the old Grand Trunk in Ontario $22,000,000 cash and $122,000,000 credit for the Grand Trunk Pacific, with the result that the Grand Trunk became bankrupt and was not able to carry out its solemn agreement with the Harbour Commission. Now the party of the first part, the city of Toronto, has fulfilled its contract with the government;-and in making these comments this morning I want to have it understood that I am not criticising the present government, because I say that all governments since 1913 have treated this agreement as a mere scrap of paper.
Another contract was entered into with the city in connection with the sale of the lot on which the new union station stands. The Grand Trunk purchased a lot in 1905 and agreed to build an up-to-date station, and subsequently became a party to the erection of a viaduct on the waterfront so that the trains might be brought in that way and the city get the benefit of a proper terminal. The viaduct agreement has not been carried out either; like the rest, it has been treated is so much waste paper. It is signed by the four parties to the contract and it provides a penalty of $100 a day during the time of the failure of any of the parties to implement it. That penalty, accumulating from 1913, has now run into hundreds of thousands of dollars which the city could collect if it wanted to take steps in the matter. The city has no desire to institute legal proceedings, but the people of Toronto are absolutely tired of the way this whole question has been ignored. After ten years of waiting they are now impatient, and they are clamouring for proper treatment. When passengers arrive at the station they are treated like a lot of cattle. There are sixteen tracks across the waterfront at Cherry street, and almost as many at York and Bay streets. The level crossings are an eyesore to the city, and after the expenditure of such a large sum as $20,000,000 to prepare the right-of-way for the railway, it is not to be wondered at if the residents of the city of Toronto are now exasperated. Some of the tenants along the waterfront have been simply driven into liquidation through the failure of the parties to this agreement to observe their part of the undertaking. The railways cannot handle the business on these tracks, either in respect of passenger traffic or in the matter of freight. During the Exhibition 165 trains were assembled at the union station in the rush period, and this will given hon. members some idea of the state of congestion there at the present time.
I would point out to the government that after all it is only a short-sighted policy on the part of the National Railways to delay the execution of this contract, for if a proper terminal were provided for the people it would increase the receipts from freight and passenger traffic. The agreement it is estimated will call for an expenditure of $32,000,00, to which the city of Toronto is liable to contribute one-third. That $32,000,000 is made up in the following way:	The new
station, including land, represents an expenditure of $9,500,000. That sum has already been spent. For land damages, the sum of $7,500,000 was to be provided; and the amount to be spent on the viaduct construction was fixed at $16,000,000. As I say, the first item of $9,000,000 odd has been spent so that there is only approximately $22,000,000 remaining to be expended, of which the city of Toronto is to provide one-third. And the city is ready and willing to-morrow to put up its share if the Railway Board will proceed with their part of the contract. Now there is no use in the government going around a circle in this matter. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) made some reference the other day to Sir Henry Thornton in connection with this question. Well, I do not think that there is any room for argument, nor has either the Railway Board or Sir Henry Thornton, any option, so far as this contract is concerned. Here is a specific agreement to which we have the seal of the company; and neither Sir Henry Thornton nor the Railway Board can set it aside. A contract is a contract, and all that is required in this case is that parliament shall provide the money which is called for. The representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Harbour Commission, the city of Toronto, and the Grand Trunk have held between twenty and thirty meetings in an endeavour to adjust the dispute. We inquired of the directors of the Grand Trunk what their stand in the matter was, and they informed us that they could do nothing. They said: "You have your contract; get the government to carry it out". Let me inform the House that we will carry out our part of the contract if parliament will provide the money to enable the railways to do their share. There is absolutely no use in vacillating on this question until Sir Henry Thornton comes back. Sir Henry Thornton, in the first place, is not a cure-all for the transportation ills of this country; and in any event the contract should be carried out. Why should the government have to wait for Sir Henry Thornton?

As I have stated before, there is only one course open to the government, and that is to include in the estimates a sum sufficient to begin the operations necessary under the National Railways' part of the contract. The Canadian Pacific Railway declared the other day that they were ready to carry out their bargain, and the Mayor of the city expressed the same preparedness. The citizens of Toronto are absolutely disgusted at the way this contract has been ignored, and visitors to the city are impressed in any but a favourable way. Besides this, there is considerable damage being caused the business interests of the city through the failure of the government to observe its agreement. Lands on which we could get factories established are lying idle simply because the Grand Trunk will not make a move in this matter. Surely the Harbour Commission and those persons who are interested must have some recourse against the government for the damages they have sustained. They have been out their rentals from this $20,000,000 worth of revenue producing property. They have not been able to get any revenue from it, and are now drawing on capital with the result that deficits are being piled up. The people of Toronto are sustaining damages and cannot get the use of their own property. In England, in Australia and in the United States the railway legislation provides a summary remedy for situations similar to this; any municipality can enforce a contract with the railway corporation in the event of failure on the part of the latter to carry out its terms. But to-day in Canada the railways are altogether supreme. They can go into a municipality, enter into a contract and then ignore it, interfere with trade and commerce, occasion damage and ruin to business, drive people into liquidation, and apparently be immune from the consequences of their actions. That is the condition of affairs as we have it in Toronto at the present time.
In 1913, an act was passed, as Chapter 26, 1 and 2 of George V to consolidate the acts relating to the harbour of Toronto. By this act the docks were to be moved into the bay and new bulkheads and pierheads were to be built. The Minister of Public Works of that day, the Hon. Mr. Rogers, stated that the Harbour Commission would have to start building their works before the government would undertake any expenditures. The Harbour Commission then spent $20,000,000 The government, I may say, has not done so

badly so far as harbour improvement is concerned. But certainly in regard to its contract in connection with the union station it has failed miserably. An order in council was also passed by the government in 1913, providing for the carrying out of these works in the harbour, and that order in council shows that the work was to be completed in the year 1916. It was provided in the main agreement between the railways and the city that the work should begin within one month from the signing of the agreement. Up to date not a spadeful of earth has been turned towards carying out this agreement. The work was to have been finished in 1916, when we were tc have a new union station with elevated tracks across the waterfront. Seven years have elapsed and nothing has been done. It is not a question of law. The agreement has been validated by legislation, and althrough the railway companies appealed the judgment of the Railway Commission, the Privy Council declared it to be binding on all parties.
I regret that at this late stage of the session I have not an opportunity of laying all the facts before hon. members, because this is the only body that can give the people of Toronto the relief which the viaduct agreement provides for. The Grand Trunk Railway Company is a party to the agreement, and in the opinion of eminent counsel who have been consulted, the government of Canada are the successors and assigns of the company. It is no use now to refer us to Sir Henry Thornton and the directors of the Canadian National Railways. We were referred to the Grand Trunk Railway Company by Sir Robert Borden when he was Prime Minister, but repeated interviews with the Grand Trunk directorate and officials extending over a period of ten years did not bring us the slightest satisfaction. The city of Toronto has been treated very unfairly in this matter. Instead of building sundry branch lines for the Canadian National Railways that will not be revenue-producing for some years to come at least, I think the government would have been better advised to carry out this viaduct agreement, for the works covered by it would more than pay fixed charges.

Does not my hon. friend know that the whole reason for the delay was that the Grand Trunk could not finance their share?
That was the excuse and possibly the reason.
Does not my hon. friend know it?

I would not say-

Supply-Toronto Viaduct
Does not my hon. friend know this further that his own directors have said that it is entirely that question, entirely a question for the government to say whether they will finance it?

In a measure my hon. friend may be correct. To come back to the question, my hon. friend's suggestion and that of the other hon. gentleman is that the government without the recommendation of the Canadian National Railway Board should proceed to put a vote in the estimates to complete this work whether the board want it or not. I say that whatever negotiations are carried on and whatever arrangements are come to should be arrived at as between the companies. Following that, it is true that if any work is to be done the parliament of Canada would have to pass a vote for the purpose, but for parliament to pass the vote before something was decided upon as between the city of Toronto and the companies, and I understand that negotiations are going on continually, would be the wrong way of going about it. But I do not want to continue the discussion. My hon. friend from South York has taken a different view. I do not know whether he wants to take the tracks up to the Donlands or not, but there is something in his view that the whole trackage should be removed from the waterfront and an entrance made farther north. It is said that in a multitude of counsel there is wisdom, but when the counsel is so conflicting I do not know that I can get much wisdom out of it.
I want my hon. friend to understand that I did not for one moment abandon the rights of the city of Toronto to the construction of the viaduct.

I am not sure that my hon. friend if he adheres to the viaduct, could make out a good case for the removal of the tracks from the waterfront because that is the purpose of the viaduct. If the tracks were removed to the north the viaduct would not be required. This is a very large question and I agree absolutely that it does not alone interest the city of Toronto, it interests all the travelling public passing in and out of this great centre of the province of Ontario, which is the city of Toronto. The traffic originating in and around Toronto and in the province of Ontario is I presume the largest traffic of any province of the Dominion for the Canadian National Railways, and I am in hopes that before very long something will be arrived at of a definite
nature between the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and the city of Toronto so that the situation may be alleviated. Generally speaking at the present moment the work would not be a productive expenditure, but the traffic is increasing so rapidly in that particular centre that there should be a method of handling that great traffic that would save annual expenditure, and in that way be productive, because the traffic particularly, is handled at risk of life and the expense of handling traffic must be greater than it would be in a well conducted terminal. We have a station there costing I think my hon. friend said 89,000,000.
The station was $4,000,000. The original viaduct was to be 89,000,000.
Up to the present time, I am told, the station has cost 86,000,000, and in addition to that the government contributed some 82,000,000 for a postal station.

May I ask a question? The position taken by the city is that they want the contract carried out. They want the viaduct, the whole viaduct and nothing but the viaduct and that they will not consent to the new station being opened until they get the viaduct. Could the minister tell the House whether his law officers advise that the government is a party to the contract as standing in the shoes of the Grand Trunk Railway the party of the second part in the contract?

and being such a party the contract can be enforced by specific performance and the government taken into the Exchequer Court of Canada.

There is always a difficulty in suing a government. In the first place if we say that the government becomes a party to the contract in place of the Grand Trunk, suit could not be entered against the government except by consent, that is by fiat, and that sometimes is not so easy to get. The better way is to have this thing straightened out amicably if possible, rather than by reference to the Exchequer Court. My hon. friend has asked me a question. I say that the situation so far as responsibility is concerned is not changed one iota by the transfer of the Grand Trunk stock. The Grand Trunk as a corporation is part of the Canadian National Railways, and the Canadian National assumes the responsibility formerly assumed by the Grand Trunk. There is therefore no change in the relationship of the Grand Trunk although the government is the shareholder.
Supply-Toronto Viaduct

As my hon. friends can understand, it is difficult to give a definite statement. I hope that when the president of the Canadian National returns from the West and the president of the Canadian Pacific from across the sea they will get together with the city of Toronto at close range and discuss this matter with the hope of coming to some amicable arrangement by which the situation in Toronto can be relieved.
My hon. friend from Quebec county (Mr. Lavigueur) made an eloquent plea this morning for the city of Quebec. I do not wish to go into details, but to express the view that I have great sympathy with him when he said that the original plans for the terminals at the city of Quebec were far superior to the ones later adopted.

The advocacy of the hon. members from Toronto in the interests of their city reminds me of a duty, that I should bring to the attention of the Minister of Railways the fact that on lesser scale but in serious measure we have a corresponding situation in the town of Truro, the chief town of the constituency which I have the honour to represent. I shall be thankful if I am not told to go to the Railway Board, and if I go to it I shall be thankful if I am not sent back to the Minister of Railways; and I am speaking partly from surmise and partly from experience. Tennyson in his "Vision of Sin" describes a voice that came from a clear sky and in very clear tones but in language that no man could understand, and I am a little afraid of that mystery when I press for the rights of the town of Truro corresponding with the rights for which the hon. members for Toronto are pressing. Some who love that town regard it as a miniature of Toronto, with streets and physical characteristics resembling Toronto's, with the instincts and temperament of its people resembling those of the people of Toronto, and that to some extent would constitute a compliment in the opinions of some hon. members. On the other hand, by pointing out the resemblance, I run the risk of keeping away from Truro some of my good friends elsewhere in this parliament. The town of Truro has a population of about eight thousand, and it has those deadly level crossings in a very important and central part of the town. One of the hon. members for Toronto put forth the fact that the holiday seekers in his city were compelled to cross the tracks there to get to a picnic resort, which I appreciate not as a luxury but as a necessity. But a still greater necessity obtains in my own town because hundreds of the homes

are so situated that little, children have to cross some half dozen pairs of rails to get to school, and during the hours of their absence you can well imagine that the hearts of their mothers are suffering very unfair and very real anxiety.
The traffic is such that a subway is very urgently needed. The freight shed, wisely or unwisely, was put upon the side of the rails whereby it is necessary to haul the freight over these tracks. In the winter-time the snow is often missing from the tracks, and besides the inhumanity to the horses engaged in hauling the freight there is considerable loss in time, worry, wear and tear connected with the hauling, to use language which is mild in the very extreme, and to say nothing of multiplied danger in this freight traffic. This matter has been agitated for some time. Now and then a life is snuffed out on these rails just as is the case in Toronto. I do not think there is any fear that a great catastrophe will happen in the sense of a number of lives being lost by any one happening. I think that happening is just about as remote in the modern town where I live as in the great city of Toronto, or vice versa; but, Mr. Speaker, there is that continual danger present to individuals, and there is the periodical loss of life, the importance of which of course we cannot exaggerate. At a country crossing, where a driver is passing with a team of horses or automobile, we can with some fairness say that it is up to him to exercise due vigilance and allow nothing to distract his attention with some possible reverence we may say that an accident would be the driver's fault. But the matter is entirely different in a city like Toronto, or even in a town like Truro. In the case of persons coming home hurriedly, chatting in groups or wearied with the exertions of the day, it may be found that temporarily the human machinery has broken down and the necessary precautions may not be observed. There may be a lapse of memory due to causes that cannot be exactly analyzed. As lives have been sacrificed in Toronto and Truro at these level crossings in the past just as surely will such losses occur in the future. If the question of expenditure is involved in providing protection, the conditions are in favour of more prompt action in Truro than in Toronto, because in Truro it is not a matter of the expenditure of millions or even of hundreds of thousands to place a subway there which will serve the public. I commend this matter to the minister as being an entirely worthy and necessary object. I only regret having taken up even this much time

Might I ask the minister
whether he could not arrange to be present at the proposed conference in Toronto on the matters we discussed this morning?

All that I can say is that I will try to be present.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY WITH THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: May I ask permission, Mr. Speaker, to return to government notices of motion in order to take up the resolution which appears in my name with respect to the Northern Pacific Halibut Fishery treaty?

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY WITH THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: By unanimous consent.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (.Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY WITH THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Resolved by the	 House of Commons:-
That it is expedient that Parliament do approve of the treaty between His Majesty and the United States of America providing effective measures for the preservation of the halibut fishery of the Northern Pacific ocean, which was signed at Washington on the second day of March, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three, a copy of which has been laid before parliament, and which was signed on behalf of His Majesty, acting for Canada, by the plenipotentiary therein named, and that this House do approve of the same.
He said: On March 6th, my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) laid on the Table of the House a copy of a treaty between His Majesty the King and the United States with respect to the preservation of the halibut fishery on the Pacific coast. This treaty was signed on March 2nd, at Washington by plenipoten-liaries representing the parties thereto. The purpose of the present resolution is to obtain from parliament approval of the [DOT] provisions of the treaty. The treaty provides for a close season for halibut in the waters contiguous to the Pacific coast in the United States and in Canada. The period of the close season is three months, from November to February, to be observed over a period of five years. Either party may be at liberty, on two years' notice, to terminate the convention at any time after the five years has expired.
There is another provision in the treaty to the effect that halibut caught in those waters during the time that the convention obtains may be used for the purposes of food by the crews of vessels, fishing for other kinds of fish. If any quantity should be caught, the treaty provides that after being brought to the shore, they shall be transferred at once to officers of the Marine department of either Canada or the United States, and disposed of by those officers at such price as they may be eble to obtain. The purpose of this provision is to do away with any element of profit in the catch of halibut and thereby remove all
Halibut Fishery Treaty

incentive to fishing for halibut during the close season.
The treaty contains a further provision for the establishment of an International Fisheries Commission to study the life history of the halibut, and to make recommendations to the governments of the two countries with respect to measures that may be required by way of the better preservation of this important natural resource. The treaty contains a clause to the effect that the governments of the two countries shall introduce legislation to make effective its provisions.
I may say that the treaty has already been assented to by the Senate of the United States, so assented to on March 4 of this year and recommended for ratification by that body, subject to a reservation which appears in the resolution assenting to the treaty. I shall read to the House the resolution itself:
Resolved (two-thirds of the senators present concurring therein) that the Senate advise and consent to the ratification of Executive D, sixty-seventh congress, fourth session, convention between the United States and Great Brtiain, signed March 2, 1923, for the preservation of the halibut fishery of the northern Pacific ocean, including the Behring sea, subject to the .understanding, which is hereby made a part of this resolution of ratification, that none of the nationals and inhabitants and vessels and boats of any other part of Great Britain shall engage in halibut fishing, contrary to any of the provisions of this treaty.
In so far as we have learned the circumstances, it would appear that the "understanding" was added at the last moment, the treaty receiving the Senate's assent only on the last day of the recent session of congress. Apparently the reservation was thought necessary because of a fear expressed by a senator from one of the western states that while the citizens and vessels of Canada would be controlled ships coming from Great Britain not being included in this prohibition, their owners might feel free to fish for halibut in these waters. However, what was overlooked in that regard was the fact that legislation which will be introduced by both the government of the United States and the government of Canada to prohibit fishing during the period of the close season will provide that not only shall the nationals of the countries concerned not have the right to fish in the prohibited area but that the citizens of every country shall be prohibited from operating from a Canadian or an American base or from attempting anything by way of halibut fishing in those waters. If they are unable to find a base on the Pacific coast, either in the United States or in Canada, it is hardly likely that the citizens of any country would be able to carry on fishing operations in northern Pacific waters.

The legislation which will be introduced by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to give effect to the provisions of this treaty will render it immediately apparent to the members of the United States Senate that the reservation they have attached as a condition to ratification is wholly unnecessary. We feel satisfied that under these circumstances the reservation will be withdrawn and the treaty assented to and ratified as it stood at the time it was signed.
I may disclose to the House evidence of the apparent haste in which the reservation was prepared by drawing attention to the wording. It reads as follows:
That none of the nationals and inhabitants and vessels and boats of any other part of Great Britain shall engage in halibut fishing contrary to any of the provisions of this treaty.
If the expression "any other part of the British Empire" had been used, it would not have been open to exception. However, the intention is perfectly plain, namely, that of preventing the citizens of any other part of the British Empire from availing themselves of fishing rights which will be denied the citizens of Canada by the terms of the treaty. We hold that the intention has always been that the prohibition should extend beyond the citizens of Canada or the British Empire to apply to citizens of any country in any part of the world. Such will be the effect as soon as the contemplated concurrent legislation is passed.
I need only add in conclusion that, as will be apparent from the reading of the treaty, its provisions relate wholly to matters which, to all intents and purposes, are of exclusive concern to the United States and Canada. The two countries might effect without a treaty, by concurrent legislation as is intended, practically all that is proposed here. Inasmuch, however, as it was thought advisable to have on record the understanding of the governments in this matter, the governments of our respective countries decided to have their commitments given the form of a treaty. I believe the terms proposed are so manifestly in the interests of the country that parliament will readily give its approval to the treaty.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: The motion, I understand, is a motion adopting the resolution which appears on page 5. I wish at this stage to make a very few comments on the general question, and will reserve more detailed treatment perhaps-

If the hon. member will allow me, it is by a clerical error that this

Halibut Fishery Treaty
matter has been placed on the order paper as one to be considered in committee of the whole. It is a simple resolution presented to the House; so that if the right hon. member has any remarks to make, he should make them now.

I understood there was an error in the order paper. I desire first of all to read the resolution, which says:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the treaty between His Majesty and the United States of America providing effective measures for the preservation of the halibut fishery of the Northern Pacific ocean, which was signed at Washington on the second day of March, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three, a copy of which has been laid before parliament, and which was signed on behalf of His Majesty, acting for Canada, by the plenipotentiary therein named', and that this House do approve of the same.
I am not discussing at the moment anything connected with the matter of the treaty, but rather certain extraordinary circumstances that attended the preparations for and the execution thereof. These circumstances ate called attention to by the wording of the resolution itself. Hon. members will observe that the resolution declares that the treaty was signed "on behalf of His Majesty the King acting for Canada, by the plenipotentiary therein named, and that this House do approve of the same." I think the records of parliament will be searched in vain for any previous reference to His Majesty the King executing a treaty "acting for" Canada by the plenipotentiary. If it is merely a misplacement of the phrase, and if the words "acting for Canada" should appear after the word "plenipotentiary"-and I really do not know why they are not there, in a resolution of such importance as this-the effect is that the plenipotentiary in the execution of the treaty acted for His Majesty the King as a representative of Canada. His Majesty the King did not for Canada. The authority given the representative of His Majesty in the document on which he bases his right to sign clearly states:
Hon. Ernest Lapointe, one of our counsel, learned in the law, member of the parliament of Canada, member of our Privy Council for Canada, Minister of Marine and Fisheries of our Dominion of Canada, have named, made, constituted and appointed, as we do by these presents name, make, constitute and appoint him our undoubted commissioner, procurator and plenipotentiary, giving to him all manner of power and authority to treat, adjust and conclude with such minister or ministers as may be vested with similar power and authority on the part of our good friends the United States of America.
The treaty undoubtedly affects chiefly the Dominion of Canada and the United States; it is an exaggeration to say that it affects solely the Dominion of Canada and the'United
284i
States. Our treaty with France respecting the tariff was a treaty which affected solely the Dominion of Canada and France; there were no others directly or indirectly bound thereby, and no others affected by the treaty as such. But here the case is different. Had it been a case where we alone had been affected it is nevertheless true, and in my judgment it is important to observe that anyone named by Canada and given his credentials by His Majesty the King executes that treaty as a representative of His Majesty the King-but in respect of Canada. I observe by the correspondence that the government attempted in the first place to make the treaty without so far as the title is concerned the interposition of His Majesty at all. The treaty as submitted by the United States of America was styled in the following language:
Convention between the United States of America and Great Britain concerning halibut fishery.
In the communication from the present government to the United States, and as well in that to the British government, it was insisted that the words "Great Britain" should be changed and the words "Dominion of Canada" substituted, although every previous treaty had been made between the United States, if that was the country, and His Majesty, the King. The error of this step on the part of the present government was pointed out and they yielded the point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think my right hon. friend wishes to misrepresent the facts.
Nor have I done so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is he referring now to the nominal heading affixed to the convention, which nominal heading was drafted by the United States government, or is he referring to what is vital and material, namely, the sections of the treaty that refer to matters executive?

I am referring to precisely what I said. In the title of the treaty submitted by the United States government in the first place the heading was:
Convention between the United States of America and Great Britain concerning the halibut fishery.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Which is the
meaningless part of the treaty.

The Prime Minister says that this is of no importance; but at the time he considered it sufficiently important to have his government address a message to the British Ambassador at Washington, for transmission, of course, in which the government
Halibut Fishery Treaty

took the stand that the words "Dominion of Canada" should be substituted for "Great Britain" in the heading. The government should have known, and I think it did know, that all treaties are made between His Majesty and whatever other country is affected thereby. Pursuing the matter, and on request that credentials be given and full authority be accorded, as was quite proper, to the representative of Canada to sign the treaty on behalf of His Majesty, this authority was immediately given; and then the notification came, no doubt in the usual way, from the British Ambassador, that the terms of the treaty being agreed to on the part of the United States and Canada he was given authority to sign and was prepared to sign along with Hon. Ernest Lapointe, who had been endowed with full authority from His Majesty. This, however, appeared to affront the dignity of the government or of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) and objection was immediately taken to that hon. gentleman having anyone else sign the treaty along with him. I note, with some regret the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) from the House during this discussion. Thq Minister of Finance, associated with the Minister of Marine, had previously negotiated without any great success, a treaty with France, and in the execution of that treaty and in the arrangements looking to its completion they had associated with them the British Ambassador to France, as in the case of Italy, the British Foreign Minister. When the terms of that treaty were under discussion I referred to this feature of the matter and the Minister of Finance very frankly stated that he approved of the association of the British Ambassador in British treaties and of his signature thereto whether those treaties affected a single dominion or affected the Empire as a whole; and he acknowledged the great assistance given by the British Ambassador in connection with the treaty. But when it comes to this Halibut Treaty the Minister of Marine and Fisheries declines to have the British Ambassador associated with him, and in this attitude he is supported by the government. He wants the signature of the Hon. Ernest Lapointe to stand alone as executory to that treaty; and representations to this effect were made persistently both to the British Ambassador and overseas until a message was despatched by the present Secretary of State for the Colonies to this government-after very many messages had been sent across from Canada, all representing that the greatest speed was necessary and that the 
treaty should be signed without delay-a message, I say, was finally despatched by the Secretary of State for the Colonies in certain terms which I shall now look up. I am now turning over a multitude of pressing epistles from the present government urging the point and asking for a hurried decision. Then I come to the message to which I have referred, dated the first of March, 1923.
With reference to your telegram of February 28 regarding the Halibut Treaty the wishes of your ministers are being telegraphed to his Majesty's Ambassador at Washington by the Secretary ef State for Foreign Affairs.
Not desiring to continue a somewhat undignified controversy with the Canadian government as to preserving the historic form of execution of treaties and at the same time loath to proclaim that hereafter there shall be no unity of action at all in so far as foreign policy and foreign treaties are concerned the Secretary of State for the Colonies, acting for the British government, stated merely that the British government had telegraphed the wishes of the Canadian government to the British Ambassador at Washington; whereupon the hurry of the previous weeks was consummated, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries hied himself to Washington and had the exceeding and unprecedented honour of executing this treaty alone without being impinged upon in that glory by the presence of the signature of the British Ambassador. The British Ambassadors, as do the ambassadors of all countries, in keeping with historic custom, necessarily take a special part in the negotiations for and the execution of treaties with the countries to which they are accredited, and never has any exception been asked for, never has any exception been made until we come to this occasion of the execution of the Halibut Treaty. I wonder how much better off we are. Is our autonomy in the smallest degree enlarged? Does anyone understand just how we are advantaged by the supreme glory of having the Minister of Marine and Fisheries execute this treaty alone, having, figuratively speaking, kicked the British Ambassador out of the door in the execution of a treaty with a foreign power?
All the while the reasons given by the government in the negotiations were to the effect that Canada alone was interested, that the treaty was one which solely concerned this Dominion and no other part of the Empire. And no sooner was the treaty executed than there was the addition of a clause by the Senate of the United States bringing in the subjects of the whole Empire and although

Halibut Fishery Treaty
there was a fearful hurry up to the 1st March, the very stars in their courses were going-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend uses the expression that the reservation of the Senate brought in all the subjects of the British Empire. The words in the Senate reservation are, "every part of Great Britain." Does he say that this expression includes all other parts of the Empire?

Undoubtedly that is the intent of the Senate. Does anyone think that the Senate intends their reservation to apply to the residents of the British Isles alone, and not to the subjects of the Empire generally, as all other treaties have applied before? But the point is not of any importance to my argument anyway. The fact is that the reservation of the Senate brings in some other parts of the Empire. That is enough for my point at present. Although there was all this precipitate hurry up to the 1st March, we have since gone through nearly four months before any desire is evinced to bring forward the treaty for ratification. There has been no treaty in operation yet. I suppose the reason for the delay is because the Senate reservation completely destroyed the pedestal upon which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries wished to stand. Now we are asked to ratify the treaty. We are going to prorogue this week, and we are asked to ratify the treaty and accept the devout hope expressed by the Prime Minister that the Senate will yet retrace its steps and not make any special reservation applicable to other parts of the Empire. It would have been well, I think, if the grounds of this hope had been given. I do not think that intrinsically the matter is of such colossal consequence.
I do wonder what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries thought was going to be gained by this act with reference to signature by the British Ambassador which, if you do not call it discourteous, so nearly approaches discourtesy that the term applies as well as any other that can be thought of. Quite clearly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) holds a distinctly different view, as do other members of the government. What is the intention? Is this treatment to continue to be accorded the British Ambassador? Are these petitions to the door of the British government to be made in respect of future treaties? Canada has for years been not only engaged in but in charge of all negotiations concerning the terms of any treaty in which she is specially or solely interested. All that is ever done by the British Ambassador, I presume, is to see that any proposed treaty
contains no terms that affect such general policy as all parts of the Empire are interested in. This being conceded as having been the practice for years, what more do we want? Why should we continue this process of offering one affront after the other in order, if possible, to magnify and emphasize before the world our desire to dissociate ourselves from the Empire in general?
We are in something of a quandary now. We are legislating, according to this bill, against Canadian fishing even on the high seas, as to w'hich, as it involves extra-territorial jurisdiction, we have no legislative power at all. Let me repeat:	As to which,
being extra-territorial, we have as yet- though I think we should have, as respects our own citizens-no authority at all. We are legislating as well that no other subjects of the British Empire shall operate there, or if they do, they cannot use our ports. In effect, we are trying now to meet the American reservation by denying indirectly the right of any British subjects to carry on these fisheries in the close season in our own as well as in extra-territorial waters.
Now, I do not deny that the objects of the treaty can only be met by making it applicable to all British subjects. Undoubtedly from the beginning Great Britain should have been associated with us, so that we would be in a position to defend our course of legislating to the best of our power to make the treaty so universally applicable. As the reser vation stands, the execution of the treaty b>
His Majesty will bind British subjects. -Is it the intention that the Australian parliament shall ratify the treaty?
No.

I do not know what the idea of the government is in this regard. As far as this feature is concerned, I am not making any particular criticism. My criticism is directed against the unnecessary and, to my mind, indelicate action by this government with relation to the historic form of executing treaties in which this country is chiefly interested.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose it is in order for me to give a resume of what preceded the negotiations which led up to the signature of this treaty. We have on the Pacific coast of this continent the greatest halibut fishery in the world, though it has been considerably diminished through over-fishing. The fishery started in 1888, and the industry has made wonderful progress in the interval, halibut being the best fish we have for shipping in fresh condition.
Halibut Fishery Treaty

In 1913 or 1914 it was discovered that vast numbers of halibut go to the banks of Alaska during the winter time, and following that discovery winter fishing started on a considerable scale. To take halibut at that season of the year is especially destructive as the fish are then in a spawning condition, and from the reproduction standpoint their capture should not be allowed. Furthermore, the flesh is then in bad condition. This winter fishery is carried on at the worst season of the year, and it is then that all the accidents to the vessels occur. In addition to that, on account of the very rough weather thea prevailing, the vessels engaged lose about fifty per cent of their equipment. And when it is borne in mind that the lines of every big vessel run to a length of forty-eight miles, with hooks at every ten feet, it will be realized what a heavy loss this entails, as also a loss of fish, because halibut at that time bite with avidity, and the dead fish pollute the fishing grounds.
The fisheries yield about fifty million pounds each year, of which about nine million pounds are taken by Canadian vessels, the greater proportion being taken by American vessels. But owing to the greater proximity of the Canadian cpasts, seventy per cent of the fish caught by American vessels is shipped by the Canadian railways. So it is very important from many viewpoints that this halibut fishery should be protected.
In 1918 an international commission was appointed by the United States and Canada to study the condition of the fishery. At that time many special war measures were in effect in both countries, and as one of these the commission recommended the adoption of two treaties, one concerning the Fraser river run of salmon, and the other, among other things, this close season for the protection of the halibut fisheries. The first treaty was negotiated, was signed, but was not ratified by the Senate of the United States; the second treaty was drafted but was never signed. Meanwhile the fisheries authorities of both countries, though they were not in accord on some other points, were in agreement on this question of the necessity of a close season for the protection of halibut on the Pacific coast, and the suggestion was made that a special treaty be negotiated and signed to provide for that close season, quite independently of the other recommendations of the international commission. The United States government approached the government of Canada in the matter of the negotiation of that treaty; in fact, they drafted a treaty and s'ent it to Canada for the consider-

ation of this government. This treaty, after the making of a few modifications, was signed, and it is the treaty which is now submitted for the approval of the House. As I have stated, it was drafted by our friends of the United States, not by us. Then, as my right hon. leader said, when the treaty came before the United States senate, a reservation was added that it should apply to the nationals of any part of the British Empire. The treaty was signed three days before the end of the term of congress; in fact, the term of congress expired the following Sunday-its last legislation was adopted on Sunday morning. The treaty was submitted in a great hurry and it is more than likely that this little rider, added at the last minute, was not given the consideration which would have been given it had the treaty been submitted at an early stage of the session.
We do not wish, after considering everything, to accept this reservation, for obvious reasons; though by the legislation which will be enacted the same purpose will be served, the same end will be reached. The legislation which both countries will adopt will make it impossible for the nationals of any country to carry on fishing operations1 in the waters covered by the treaty. In the first place, there is no discussion possible as to our right to prohibit halibut fishing in the territorial waters within the three mile limit; that will apply to the world. We have not the right or the power to prevent anybody from fishing in the extra-territorial waters, but it is physically impossible for any vessel to carry on halibut fishing operations in Pacific waters without using as a base either American ports or Canadian ports. So that the mere closing of our ports and the closing of American ports to fishing vessels during the close season will make it impossible for any national, the citizen of any country, to carry on fishing operations there.
Then, I may be asked, why should the reservation nqt be accepted? If we were to accept it we would have to submit the treaty for ratification to all the parliaments of the British Empire. We cannot bind the Australians or the New Zealanders not to fish in extra-territorial waters off our coast any more than we can bind the citizens of any foreign country not to do so; the only way that we can prevent it is by closing our ports, and this we will do. In the second place, it would be a discrimination against British subjects, against the citizens of Australia or New Zealand. But if it were possible to carry on fish-

Is that a crime? If it is a crime I confess that I am an unrepentant sinner. Our action in this regard is in line with the logical and natural sequence of the principles which have been asserted and accepted by all responsible authorities in the British Empire for the past few years. Nowhere, perhaps, are those principles more clearly asserted than in the memorandum circulated on behalf of the Dominion prime ministers in March, 1919, which I take from the British Year Book of International law for 1922-1923, page 32. The Canadian Prime Minister and the prime ministers of all the Dominions subscribed to that memorandum. Here is the language of that memorandum:
All the treaties and conventions resulting from the Peace Conference should 'be so drafted as to enable the Dominions to become parties and signatories thereto. This procedure will give suitable recognition to the part played at the Peace Table by the British Commonwealth as a whole, and will, at the same time, record the status attained there by the Dominions. The procedure is .in consonance with the principles of constitutional government that obtain throughout the Empire. The Crown is the Supreme Executive in the United Kingdom and in all the Dominions, but it acts on the advice of different ministries within different constitutional units; and under Resolution IX of the Imperial War Conference, 1917, the organization of the Empire is to be based upon equality of nationhood.
That is a fine principle and I accept it entirely as far as I am concerned. May I quote an extract from a despatch of the Canadian cabinet dated the 4th of December, 1918, to the Right Hon. Council is of opinion that in view of war efforts of Dominion other nations entitled to representation at Conference should recognize unique character of British Commonwealth composed of group of free nations under one sovereign and that provision should be made for special representation of these nations at conference.

Russia is not a party to the Treaty and has not been called upon to consider the question, but when she does one need not apprehend any dissent from her; there remains only the United States.
Now, I claim that by signing and accepting the signature of Canada on that treaty the United States have recognized the international status of Canada, and it should not be the part of Canadians to criticize that status.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me. Why did he permit the British Ambassador to sign the French treaty?

I have given the opinions of some of our distinguished public men who were members of the government at the time. May I now give the opinion of constitutional authorities on the new status acquired by the Dominions. I have here an extract from an article in the British Year Book of International Law for the year 1922-23, by Dr. Malcolm M. Lewis, lecturer on international law in England, page 33. It says:
This process was carried a step further in the procedure adopted for securing ratification of the Treaty, which was debated and approved by each Dominion parliament and was ratified for it, not on the advice and responsibility of the government of the United Kingdom, but on the advice and responsibilty of the Dominion government concerned.
The Dominions consolidated their newly acquired international status by becoming, and being recognized as, original members of the League of Nations. They are entitled to the same representation in the Assembly of the League as sovereign states, and there is no legal obstacle to one or more of the Dominions being elected to the Council of the League as the representatives of the Assembly. In fact, as far as the League is concerned, they have the same rights, and duties, as independent states, and these rights and duties are increased by the fact of their being appointed Mandatory States over certain former colonies of the German Empire. The Union of South Africa has been given a "C'' mandate for German South-West Africa, New Zealand for Samoa, and Australia for certain islands in the South Pacific. It is significant that these mandates were received by the Dominions direct from the Secretariat of the League of Nations, and correspondence thereon is not being conducted through the Imperial government. That this is a deliberate policy is shown by the fact that New Zealand wished to take her mandate through the Imperial government, but in consequence of the attitude adopted by South Africa and Australia all the mandates were issued direct. The dominions concerned are, therefore, responsible for their mandates not to the British government but directly to the League of Nations.
As original members of the League of Nations the dominions are also members of the International Labour Organization for which provision was made in the various treaties of peace. As such, they are entitled to direct and separate representation at all general International Labour conferences, and at the three conferences already held they have not only availed themselves of their right to be represented, but have, on occasions, indulged in cross-voting both amongst themselves and with the representatives of the British Empire.
Dr. Keith, another authority on constitutional law, says in his book "War Government in the Dominions," page 155:
In one point only did the proceedings in the matter of signature and ratification vary from the forms which would have been employed had the dominions been independent states; the Dominion plenipotentiaries were nominated and authorized to act for the dominions by their governments, but they received formal full powers to treat and sign from the King on the advice of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, and the royal ratification for the Empire was signified on the advice of the Secretary of State.
What is the difference between, the procedure, as demonstrated by Professor Keith in this article, and the procedure which has been

Each of the units is a member of the League in its own right, possessing one vote in the Assembly of the League, and the right to be represented there by not more than three delegates.
