Now, what is the opinion of British statesmen on that subject. May I quote Mr. Lloyd George. I take his words from a recent book, "The Constitution of Canada," by Mr. W. P. M. Kennedy, page 370. On the subject of the Imperial Conference of 1921 Mr. Lloyd George spoke as follows:
He expressed himself satisfied with the progress achieved through full and free consultation between the prime ministers. He welcomed the idea of a Canadian minister at Washington. He emphasized that the dominions had been accepted fully into the comity of nations by the whole world, and that they were equal partners in the dignities and the responsibilities of the British Commonwealth, with "liberty as its binding principle. . . . based not on force but on goodwill and a common understanding."
I have here the words of Mr. Bonar Law, which are perhaps more emphatic than those of Mr. Lloyd George, but I do not like to weary the House by too many quotations. I will quote the words of Lord Milner, which appear in "Canadian Constitutional Studies," page 114;	.
The only possibility of a continuance of the British Empire is on a basis of out-and-out equal partnership between the United Kingdom and the Dominions. I say that without any kind of reservation whatsoever. It is very easy to say that; but undoubtedly the working out of it in practice without bringing about the severance of relations between us and the dominions will be one of the most complicated tasks which statesmanship has ever had to face. I am not afraid of it, and yet I have to admit that the difficulties are such that our best efforts may end in failure. I hope not. At any rate there is no other way out.
The new status of the Dominion is further exemplified in a recent act of the British parliament, the constitution of the Irish Free state. In the treaty between Ireland and the United Kingdom no mention is made any longer of the British Empire, but of the British Commonwealth of nations, and here is the oath that is taken by the members of parliament of the Irish Free state under that treaty-
I do solemnly swear true faith and allegiance to the constitution of the Irish Free state as by law established and that I will be faithful to His Majesty King George V, his heirs and successors by law, in virtue of the common citizenship of Ireland with Great Britain and her adherence to and membership of the group of nations forming the British Commonwealth of nations.
Professor MacNeill, K.C., in the Journal of Comparative Legislation and International Law, page 53, says:

The establishment of the Irish Free state preserves to Ireland her position and indefeasible status as an independent nation and her entrance into the British Commonwealth of nations as an equal member of that commonwealth confirms and strengthens the status of each member of that commonwealth as an independent nation, "in the fullness", to use the words of Mr. Healy, the Governor General, "of partnership in liberty with the nations co-operating in equal membership of a great commonwealth of free peoples".
Now, Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend said that it was the first time such a thing had been dreamed of. I think I have shown that at the Peace Treaty, in the negotiations for the League of Nations, in everything that pertains to the League of Nations, the Dominions act on their own behalf. It was an international convention, signed by many countries of the world. Great Britain signed, through many gentlemen who are mentioned Lord Mersey was the president of the British delegation. I understand this is mentioned by Mr. Keith in his work on Dominion governments. At the Radiotelegraph Conference in 1912 the delegates sat there and signed alone for their dominions, as the British delegates signed for the rest of the British Empire. In order to show that we have not done anything so revolutionary in that matter, may I say that what has been done has been according to the practice of Canadian statesmen in the past. I have here the text of a resolution moved in the House of Commons in 1882 on April 21st, 1882, by the Hon. Edward Blake, who was certainly a good Britisher and a good constitutional lawyer, and what was the motion moved by Mr. Blake? It was as follows:
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the Chair, but that it be resolved, that Canada no longer occupies the position of an ordinary dependency of the Crown; she numbers four million of free men, trained in the principles of constitutional government'; she comprises one-half of the North American Continent, including seven provinces federally united under an Imperial charter, which recites that her constitution is to be similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom; and that she possesses executive and legislative authorities over vast areas in the Northwest out of which one province has already been created, and in time others will be formed.

That it is expedient to obtain all necessary powers to enable Her Majesty, through her representative, the Governor General of Canada, acting by and with the advice of the Queen's Privy Council of Canada, to enter by an agent or representative of Canada, into direct communication with any British possession or foreign State for the purpose of negotiating com-

This policy is in the best'traditions of the Liberal party. This policy is the latest link in the long chain of events which following the principles laid down by the reformers of the old times, Baldwin and Lafontaine, step by step, stage by stage have brought Canada to the position it now occupies, that is to say the rank, dignity and status of a nation within the British Empire.
As I am quoting from distinguished men, I wish to quote words from my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). In a speech which I admired very much, delivered by the right hon. gentleman when he was overseas in 1921, and which is published in his "Overseas Addresses," I find the following at page 15:
We legislate each for ourselves unfettered; we advise through separate councils a common sovereign; we confer together in order better to understand the wider overriding common interest; between a sense of independence and a sense of unity there is no clash but harmony. On these principles our own league of nations has survived, and it has served the world wonderfully well.
These are fine words, but surely they must not be merely words; we must act upon them.
But I find other words of my right hon. friend. I find them in Sir Robert Borden's book "Canadian Constitutional Studies" at pages 113 and 114. Sir Robert Borden says:
In May, 1921, the Canadian Prime Minister, in the Manchester Guardian Centenary number, May 5, 1921, declared that the relations between the constituent parts of the Empire must be based upon a conception of complete freedom and equality in national status. Further he observed that the practical need would be met by clearly understood and definitely acepted declarations of principle in so much of the form and content of the existing mechanism as may be found to be obsolete.
These, too, are fine words, and I think we acted in perfect harmony with the doctrine laid down by my right hon. friend in the position which we took in the present case. My right hon. friend declares that we were guilty of an act of discourtesy. I believe he said it was an affront; at least, it was an act of discourtesy towards the British Ambassador in Washington. Well, Sir, surely when a man is twenty-one years of age, as my right hon. friend has stated so many times that this nation is, it is not discourteous on his part to sign his promissory notes without asking his former guardian to sign with him. Is an obligation of the Canadian government to enforce regulations in Canada invalid, not binding, because it is not endorsed? We are not living in 1830; this is 1923 and everybody in this country should bear that in mind. But, Sir, I say that it was not an act of discourtesy; rather, I think it was an act of gracious courtesy on the part of his Majesty the King, to appoint Canadian men to sign Canadian treaties on his behalf. Far from impairing the unity of the Empire it strengthens it, it exemplifies it, while recognizing the autonomy of every part of the Empire.
I have heard somewhere or read in the newspapers, the silly argument that because we have not a strong navy and strong military forces we should not sign treaties. Mr. Speaker, Canada is much stronger than most of the independent nations; and force is not the only criterion of national status. We need no navy. After all, what have we done? We have contracted by this treaty to fulfil certain obligations, and we need not have any navy to fulfil our obligations. If we do not fulfil them we shall deserve whatever may come to us. Everything that has been done in Canada, and in every part of the British Empire for that matter, looking in the direction of responsible government and nationhood has always been assailed as a dangerous step; every move which has been made in this country in that respect has been made against the will

and despite the clamours of those who are apprehensive of the future and imagine destruction and separation ahead. But, Sir, the fuller the liberty that has been given the greater the unity of empire that has been accomplished. Why, when the government of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman accorded responsible government to South Africa the action was attacked in the British parliament as a foolish one. I have here the words of a great and distinguished British statesman, Lord Balfour, who at the time assailed the action of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman as the most reckless experiment that political folly had ever conceived. Yet, Mr. Speaker, that folly is accepted to-day as having been the greatest piece of wisdom that Great Britain could have displayed in that day. We need not be afraid of having more liberty provided we maintain unity; and this all Canadians desire. In conclusion, I say that the treaty which is submitted for the approval of the House has the same force, the same strength, the same validity, being signed by a Canadian, as it would have if signed by anyone else.

I am reluctant to say anything after the very eloquent and able address we have heard from the other side of the House; I rise merely to associate myself -with the ideas that have been expressed. I do not think there is an hon. member in this House who is not a perfectly loyal and true Canadian; and whatever little differences there may appear in our expressions of that loyalty, I am inclined to think that ultimately it will be found that our views are essentially the same. As one who was not bom in the Dominion of Canada I rejoice in the fact that step by step this young country is attaining to full national existence, a nation free and equal with other nations in the commonwealth. There is one encouraging circumstance that predominates in all the events that have taken place, and ir is this, that with every apparent slackening of the legal bonds that unite the various parts of the Empire there seems to be a proportionate increase in strength in the common loyalty and in the other high sentiments that are, after all, more truly representative of "the ties that bind." I fully realize that there may be some difficulties ahead of us; no doubt there will arise some troubles which it will be difficult to solve. But knowing the temper of the people of Great Britain, their generosity, their freedom-loving spirit, knowing the loyalty of Canadians and their faith in their own young nation, and believing in loyalty to that common Crown to which

we all pay fealty, I have no fear for the future. We know that no young man ever reaches the full stature of manhood until he has taken upon himself the responsibility and duties incident to manhood. And so shall it be with a nation. Until we too are ready and willing to take upon ourselves the responsibilities and duties of nationhood, Canada can never attain to that position which she should rightfully occupy. I repeat that I am only too glad to associate myself with the idea of Canada as a free and independent nation-a nation co-equal with her sister nations in the commonwealth.

The former administration had no doubt whatever as to the absolute freedom and independence of this country-of our nationhood. The only trouble, I think, we are ever likely to have with our friends opposite is this. We have the conviction that the force of this country can be best exercised in the closest co-operation with other component parts of the British Empire. We have the conviction that the British Empire is strong
when it acts as a unit. This argument as to our rights being called in question is entirely beside the issue. There is no question about it. It is one question.

I was asked a

That is what I think about our Canadian situation. I am convinced that there is something in unity, that there is still a whole lot in tradition, that there is still a whole lot in the different races of which this country is composed, that to-day we ought not to try and think that everything of the past should be discarded, but rather we should use this new nationhood of ours in such a way as to make better and stronger and more efficient the greatest influence for good that the world has ever seen-the British Empire.
Mr. VlEN: In what way did the signing of this treaty by Canadians hamper the work that my hon. friend now advocates or,hamper our progress?

I have much

As an assistant?

There is just another thing I would like to say in connection with the subject while I am on my feet. Most of our interests and most of our troubles with the United States are entirely financial; I do not mean financial *n its narrow sense but in the broad sense of the word-trade questions. I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will acquit me of any intention of speaking at any length. I hope you wall have observed the fact that most of my remarks to-day have been provoked by questions from hon. gentlemen, and I apologize for taking up the length of time I have with this impromptu statement.

Mr. Speaker, after the eloquent and exhaustive speech which has been made by
the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) on this important question it ill becomes a modest back bencher to take part at some length at this eleventh hour of the session in the discussion of this resolution, but the subject is to my mind a most important one and I believe that the arguments to support the stand taken by the government have not been exhausted. I shall therefore take the liberty of giving my views to the House on some of the points that have not yet been touched upon.
There is first a very strong argument to make it seems to me, in reviewing the development which since confederation has marked the evolution of our international relations. I will, however, relieve the House from this historical development because while it is an argument that may have some value in itself it is not very conclusive. There is, however, an appreciation of this argument which I find in a book recently published by Mr. Porritt, entitled "Fiscal and Diplomatic Freedom of the Overseas Dominions," where he makes this appreciation of these developments:
There is no law on the statute books of Westminster to support the existing diplomatic freedom of the dominions. It is a freedom, however, that may now be said to be recognized and guaranteed like so much else in the polity of Great Britain and in the polity of the Empire, by usage or the law of the constitution.
The strongest argument that I intend to make derives in my humble judgment from the position that Canada has taken in the Treaty of Peace and in the League of Nations. When the Treaty of Peace was signed at Versailles each of the self-governing dominions was represented by special delegates, distinct from those of Great Britain, having received their full powers directly from the King, on the advice of the Dominion cabinet, and acting separately each for his local government, as a separate entity.
When the League of Nations was formed, the self-governing dominions claimed and obtained the recognition of a distinct status, giving them an international existence, and were admitted into the league as separate states on the same footing as all the small independent nations, and were allowed their representatives as all the other members, the sovereignty of which was not controverted.
It may be said that from that moment a status separate and distinct from that of the Empire as a * whole was fully recognized as appertaining to the dominions by the government of Great Britain and by the foreign nations which entered the League. Who will hold now when Canada has entered the
Halibut Fishery Treaty

League of Nations as a separate entity on a footing equal to that of other full sovereign states with her distinct representation that she should not necessarily enjoy a status and a diplomatic freedom enabling her to act alone in her intercourse with foreign nations in all matters which are her exclusive concern?
No one at the time thought of denying the dominions this new status which they had fully earned by their sacrifices for the cause of the Empire. It was recognized by all the leading statesmen of the Empire. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has given quotations from Lord Milner and Mr. Lloyd George. I have another one here which I think is most important from Lieutenant-Colonel Amery then Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies and now First Lord of the Admiralty. In a speech in the House of Commons on the 30th of July 1919, he was still more explicit. He said:
That which has most impressed the outside world is the fact that at that conference-Paris-the full equality of the dominions with ourselves as nations, has been recognized not only by us but by the other governments. They have been treated not only as equal nations within the brotherhood of the British Empire but as equal nations with other nations outside the Empire and I know that there are some timid imperialists, I might perhaps call them, who think it is a beginning of the end of any effective imperial unity. My conviction is exactly to the contrary; I have always been convinced that closer imperial unity could only be based on the recognition of the fullest equality of status between ourselves and the other dominions of the Empire.
In the dominions expression is given to the *same sentiments. You hear General Smuts in an address to the people of South Africa declare that
The dominions have in principle authority and power, not only in respect to their domestic questions but also their international or foreign relations and. . . the questions of peace or war which may affect them. If a war is to affect them they will have to declare it; if peace is to be made in respect of them they will have to sign it. Their independence has been achieved.
This change in our status is to-day sanctioned by international law. In addition to what has been quoted by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries may I quote from Oppenheim's International Law, third edition:
But the position of self-governing dominions underwent a fundamental change at the end of the world war. Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and also India were not only separately represented within the British Empire delegation at the Peace conference, but also became, side by side, with Great Britain original members of the League of Nations. Separately represented in the Assembly of the League they may, of course, vote there independently of Great Britain. Now the League of Nations is not a mere administrative *mion .... but the organized family of nations. Without doubt therefore the admission of these four self-governing dominions to membership gives them a position in international law.

Now all these declarations were accepted in Canada and elsewhere as a recognition of a new order of things. This progress in our constitutional development is largely due to the untiring efforts of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and of the then Prime Minister of Canada, Sir Robert Borden; and the leaders of his party after him on many occasions emphasized this progress in this House particularly on the question of the ratification of the Peace Treaty and on that of the appointment of a Canadian Ambassador at Washington.
Is it possible in the face of all these developments of our constitutional rights, when we are told and we claim that we have acquired complete nationhood; that we are on an equality of status with any other part of the British Empire; that a partnership now exists between the different parts of the Empire-is it possible to maintain the practice of having our treaties, concerning our own particular commercial interests, having no relation whatever to any other part of the Empire-made in the name of Great Britain signed by the British Ambassador or ratified by the Crown on the advice of the Imperial cabinet?
To keep up such a practice is in my humble opinion absolutely inconsistent with the position which Canada now occupies in the family of nations and in the league; it is incompatible with the status that has been accorded to Canada; it would be a retrograde step injurious to those who have been the protagonists of our constitutional progress, and unworthy of our national dignity.
We have entered the League of Nations with our distinct representatives entitled to vote independently of those of Great Britain and even adversely to them. It is a position in which we necessarily find ourselves because if it was otherwise, the other nations by allowing the dominions a distinct status in the league, would merely have been granting Great Britain the right to have four times as many delegates in the assembly as any other membef of the league, and it is not to be presumed that it was their intention to do so.
If, after having assumed that stand, we must in our diplomatic relationships with other countries, in matters relating exclusively to Canada, act as if we were in tutelage, appear only accompanied by our guardian, and become bound by our contracts' only if they are made with the authorization of the Mother Country and signed by an Imperial delegate, distinct from the Canadian diplomatic envoy, is there a nation which will not think that Canada entered the League of Nations under false pretences and for no other

Halibut Fishery Treaty
purpose than to increase the British representation? Since we have agreed to enter the League of Nations, we are in honour bound to act as if we enjoyed complete diplomatic freedom and should get rid of all formalities which would imply a state of subordination and dependence. We are in association with the commonwealth of British nations but this should not prevent us from acting in accordance with our views and singly in matters which concern us alone. We may keep the Imperial government posted on our external relations; we may, and should, abstain from doing anything to damage or affect our co-partners, we may, and should, take the advice of the Imperial cabinet in all matters which have any bearing on the Empire at large, but all these are matters to be settled between ourselves.
In our dealings with foreign countries, regarding matters which affect Canada alone, we must act on our own behalf-without the participation of any tutor or guardian-under powers derived directly from the Crown, on the advice of the Canadian cabinet or parliament. To do otherwise would be to acknowledge a state of subjection incompatible with the status which we now occupy in the League of Nations.	.
Since the League of Nations was formed, Canada has tried to live up to her new status. When the Disarmament Conference took place at Washington in November, 1921, no invitation was sent to the dominions. The British government decided to appoint some representatives from the dominions, and was proceeding to appoint the delegates suggested by the prime ministers of the dominions when General Smuts protested against this procedure in a telegram addressed to the Canadian Premier on October 19, 1921, in which he says:
Agitation in congress against our independent voting power in the League of Nations was a direct challenge to new dominion status. It is first great international conference after Paris and if dominions concerned are not invited and yet attend, it will be a bad precedent and dominions' status will suffer. If a stand is made now and America acquiesces battle for international recognition our international status is finally won.
A copy of this telegram was sent by him to the British Premier Lloyd George, who acknowledged the truth of the statement in a wire to the Canadian Premier on 21st October, 1921, wherein he said:
I am completely in accord of course, with his (Smuts) view that dominion representatives should hold the same status as at Paris.
To which message Mr. Meighen replied on 27th October, 1921:
Essential that Dominion representatives should hold same status as at Paris and that this status must not be allowed to be prejudiced by proceedings at Washington Conference.
As it was then too late to start negotiations for a direct invitation, the procedure concerning the nomination of the Canadian representative was altered to the extent that he received his full powers from the Crown, by direction of an order in council of the Canadian cabinet, and not from the imperial cabinet. The effect of the protest was noticeable, however, at the Genoa conference which took place a few months after, when, in January, 1922, the invitation was addressed directly by the Italian Ambassador to the Prime Minister of Canada.
There is no doubt in my mind, that under her new status Canada can act alone in her dealings with foreign countries in all matters of exclusively local interest, and this view is supported by an authority like Oppenheim, who states in the .volume from which I already have quoted:
International negotiations can be conducted by all such states as have a standing within the family of nations. . . It would be wrong to maintain that states which are not fully sovereign can never be parties to international negotiations on those points concerning which they have a standing within the family of nations.
And further he says:
Not full sovereign states can become parties only to such treaties as they are competent to conclude. . .
Ordinarily a vassal state can conclude treaties concerning such matters as railways, extradition commerce and the like.
Now, what are commercial treaties? The same author thus defines them:
Commercial treaties are treaties concerning the commerce and navigation of the contracting states and concerning the subjects of those states who are engaged in commerce or navigation.
-Undoubtedly the treaty which we have before us falls within these categories, and should have been made exclusively in the name of Canada.
It is an	agreement which, to have
any	effect,	must be	implemented by
local legislation. My contention is, that under the present constitution, as it has developed since confederation, Canada has sole and exclusive jurisdiction to pass legislation to give effect to that treaty. If Canada alone could give effect to that treaty then it necessarily implies that Canada alone could make it, and that it should not only have been signed by the Canadian plenipotentiary alone, but should have been made in the name of the Dominion of Canada.
There was another reason in this particular case why the Canadian government should assert its right to act alone. The American

Halibut Fishery Treaty

government only of all the nations which have participated in negotiations which led to the formation of the League of Nations, has refused to recognize the right of the dominions to a separate and distinct representation in the league, and this opposition to dominion representation was one of the grounds upon which the United States senate rejected the league. Under these circumstances the Canadian government was well inspired in insisting that the treaty should be negotiated directly by Canada and the United States, without the intervention of the British Ambassador, because this new procedure involved, to a certain extent, the recognition by the United States of our new status, and it would have been a mistake to allow the occasion to pass without taking advantage of it.
This is in accordance with the rules of international law. Oppenheim says on this point:
A permanent diplomatic envoy needs no other empowering document than his general letters of credence, if he is not entrusted with any task outside the limits of the ordinary business of a permanent legation: but in case he is entrusted with any such task, as for instance if any special treaty or convention is to be negotiated', he requires a special empowering document, namely, "full powers."
It therefore follows that the full powers having been issued to the Canadian Minister of Marine, no other authority was required.
The action of the Canadian government m abstaining from requiring the signature of the British Ambassador, as had heretofore been the practice, did not mean any lack of consideration or courtesy to him. It was in duty bound to claim and assert the right of Canada to act under her own exclusive authority in the negotiation of her treaties. That was one way, and perhaps the only way to maintain a stand in full accord with the new position this country occupies within the comity of nations.
Some timorous people are inclined to dread the consequences which such a policy may have on our relations with the Empire. They say that the adoption of such a policy would bring about the disintegration of the Empire or would disrupt it, and that it is equivalent to a declaration of independence. As a matter of fact, I believe that is the only argument which may be brought forth against these views. But in Canada we are getting used to this argument, and experience has taught us that there is not much in it. As far back as 1837 the question of responsible government for the colonies was agitated At that time there were very strong objections to such a policy, and Lord John Russell,
fMr. Morin.]
then Prime Minister, had recourse to this high sounding argument when he wrote:
It is proposed that the executive council slhould bo made to resemble the ministry in this country. I hold this proposition to be entirely incompatible with the relations between the Mother Country and the colony. The relations between the Mother Country and the colony require that His Majesty should be represented not by a person removable by the assembly but by the governor sent by the king responsible to the king and to the parliament of Great Britain. This was the necessary constitution of a colony, and if you have not these relations existing between the Mother Country and the colony you will soon have an end' to the relations altogether.
A few years after responsible government was granted to Canada and the relations between the two countries were not affected in any way. Later, in 1859, when Galt increased the duties on British manufactured goods imported into Canada, the same argument was advanced. The Sheffield manufacturers in a memorial contended that:-
The policy of protection to native manufacturers in Canada should be distinctly discountenanced by Her Majesty's government as a system condemned by reason and experience as being directly contrary to the policy solemnly adopted by the Mother Country and calculated to breed disunion and distrust between Great Britain and her colonies.
The firm answer of Sir A. T. Galt is well known. He said:-	'
*Self-government would be utterly annihilated if the views of the Imperial government were to be preferred to those of the people of Canada. It is therefore the duty of the present government distinctly to affirm the right of the Canadian legislature to adjust the taxation of the people in the way they deem best,, even if it should unfortunately happen to meet the disapproval of the Imperial ministry. Her Majesty cannot be advised to disallow such acts unless her advisers are prepared to assume the administration of the affairs of the colony, irrespective of the views of its inhabitants.
It was this stand which finally won for Canada absolute fiscal freedom, and yet no disruption or disunion followed.
Again, you may recall the answer of the Marquis of Ripon to the demand of the colonies at the conference of 1894 to negotiate their own commercial treaties when he said that:
To grant such a right would be equivalent to breaking up the Empire into a number of independent states.
The power to negotiate treaties was conceded to Canada in 1907 and the fatal results which were predicted did not materialize in this case, any more than in the others. We are justified in stating that not only is such an argument without foundation, but the reverse proposition is nearer the truth-that the greater the freedom granted to Canada the firmer are the ties which bind this country and Great Britain together. To-day

Halibut Fishery Treaty
these ties are apparently so elastic that on the 30th of March, 1920 in the British House of Commons the Right Hon. Bonar Law could say:
There is not a man in this House who would not admit that the connection of the dominions with the Empire depends upon themselves. If the self-governing dominions, Australia, and Canada chose to-morrow to say:	We will no longer make a part of the
British Empire, we would not try to force them. Dominion home rule means the right to decide their own destinies.
And yet these ties, elastic as they are, are so strong that in the first days of August 1914, when war was declared between Great Britain and Germany, all the self-governing dominions, without being bound or even called upon to do so, but simply by a movement of their own free will, without hesitation, without discussion, flew to the side of Great Britain and fought with her, till final victory was won. Would Canada have made the sacrifices which she did make in this war if she had been compelled by a superior authority to take part in it? I believe not. No, Mr. Speaker, the argument that Canada cannot expect to enjoy a measure of sovereignty which will entitle her to make her treaties in her own name, to appoint her own commercial plenipotentiaries acting under powers derived from the King on the advice of his Canadian cabinet, without endangering the unity of the Empire is a pusillanimous one and must be set aside.
Now Mr. Speaker, some may find that I have been rash in my statements. I may have scared the "timid imperialists" of this House if there are any, but I think that we might as well face the situation squarely. At all times has our constitutional development pointed towards the goal which we have now reached; our position to-day, as I have outlined it, is the logical conclusion of the claims and actions of the former governments and of the former leaders of this House. When one studies the political history of Canada during recent times, he is astonished at finding to what extent the successive Premiers of Canada of both parties were of one mind in claiming for Canada, larger and larger powers, more and more liberties in her dealings with other nations. This movement for larger and more complete liberty has taken a new impetus on account of the war, and now I claim that Canada, by her sacrifices during the war; on account of the economic crisis through which she has to trend as a consequence of her participation in the war; by the efforts and foresight of her leaders, has acquired a status equal to that of the other small nations which compose the family of nations. I claim that this status 2851
has been acknowledged by the British government, by foreign nations and that she must not do anything which may be of a nature to prejudice that status; that on the contrary she must, on every occasion assert her right to full and complete sovereignty in her dealings with foreign nations in all matters which concern her alone.
By doing so her position in the comity of nations shall become more and more exalted and the ties which bind her to Great Britain will in no way be affected: if anything they will be strengthened because associations founded on freedom and natural inclinations are more solid and more durable than those founded on the domination of one partner and the subordination of the other.
Our actions in this respect are only in line with the aspirations of our forefathers who, as far back as 1851, in the platform of the Reform party claimed that:
Canadian commerce and commercial intercourse with other nations, should be under the control of the legislators.
They would be in accord with the conception of our aspirations, as set forth by a famous statesman Lord Elgin, who in 1850 declared that he conceived it his mission:
"To convince Canadians that without severing the bonds that united them with Great Britain, they might attain the degree of perfection and social and political development to which organized communities of freemen had the right to aspire."
If we are freemen our aim can only be freedom; freedom in our internal affairs, freedom in our commercial intercourse with other nations, the fullest freedom consistent with the maintenance of our association with the British commonwealth of nations.

I am thoroughly in accord with what the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) stated to-day, and I am also in thorough accord with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, (Mr. Lapointe). I go further and I state my justification in a few words, by quoting from two of our poets. Tennyson says that the constitutional development of our country and of our Empire
broadens slowly down From precedent to precedent.
It is a constitutional advance which can be justified by every Canadian, by every other nation or British commonwealth. I wish to quote from another poet who says:
Daughter am I in my mother's house,
But mistress in my own.
I wish to say, in regard to the future of the world, that Canada is the equal of a benign mother in this regard. As far as this con-
Halibut Fishery Treaty

tinent is concerned-and this continent has the making of a future world above any other, or equal to any other country-I say that Canada is here to stay by the grace of the United States, if they choose to accord it; but in spite of the United States if we must. When we are on this continent, the equal of any nation or power, we have the right to make our own treaties concerning this continent. We are the equal of the United States or any other nation in making treaties for ourselves, That is in line with what has been quoted here to-day from Canadian statesmen and from British statesmen, time after time. I am glad to see that almost the unanimous opinion of this House is that Canada has at least reached a national status, and that fact is recognized in the House and still more in the world at large.

There were several treaties which grew out of the war and which were signed at Versailles, and there were treaties signed	at Washington, after the conference on the Limitation of Armaments. The representative of Canada at Washington was the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, formerly Prime Minister of this country. Sir Robert was appointed representative by His Majesty the King on the recommendation of the government of my right hon. friend opposite. In preparing the order in council recommending that full power be given Sir Robert Borden as the representative of Canada at the Washington Conference on Limitation of Armaments, my right hon. friend used language which I think deserves to be quoted here. Sir Robert Borden has thought it of sufficient importance to direct the attention of the country to it in the report of the conference which he prepared for presentation to this parliament. At page 43 there will bo found the following statement by Sir Robert Borden:
For convenience of reference I also set out herewith (2) the text of the order in council sanctioning the issuance by His Majesty the King of the Full-Power necessary to provide me with authority to sign, "for and in the name of His Majesty the King in respect of the Dominion of Canada", such treaties as might be concluded at the conference-
Exactly the form and order of words to which my right hon. friend takes exception.

It is a better expression; clearly it is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, Sir
Robert Borden will no doubt be pleased to learn that the right hon. gentleman thinks the language he used is superior to that of his former leader. The order in council itself appears in the document at page 143. It is dated Thursday, the 27th day of October, 1921, at which time my right hon. friend was in office as Prime Minister. I think I had better read the entire order in council as it has a bearing on the present case. May I say that the present government, in the drafting of the order in council referred to in the resolution, followed verbatim et literatim, with the exception of the names, the wording of the particular order passed by its predecessor.
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on a report from the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs, submitting that it is expedient, in connection with the forthcoming conference on the Limitation of Armament and on Pacific and Far Eastern questions, summoned by the government of the United States to meet at Washington on November 11th, 1921, to invest fit person with full power to treat on the part of His Majesty the King in respect of the Dominion of Canada with persons similarly empowered on the part of other states, is pleased to order and doth hereby order that His Majesty the King be humbly moved to issue letters patent to the Eight Honourable Sir Robert Laird Borden, a member of His Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council, G.C. M.G., K.C., naming and appointing him as commissioner and plenipotentiary in respect of the Dominion of Canada with full power and authority to conclude with such plenipotentiaries as may be vested with similar power and authority on the part of any powers or states, any treaties, conventions, or agreements in connection with the said conference, and to sign for and in the name of His Majesty the King in respect of the Dominion of Canada everything so agreed upon and concluded and to transact all such other matters as may appertain thereto.
I think, when we realize that the procedure in international matters respecting treaties was gone into very carefully by Sir Robert Borden and those associated with him at the time, our government might have justly been held remiss had we without good cause taken what I might describe as a backward step in asserting the manner in which this country should be represented in negotiating a treaty which has to do solely with its neighbour and iteslf.	_
The next point my right hon. friend ventured to criticize was a change in the wording of the draft. Nothing appears to have been too small for him to call attention to. The wording to which my right hon. friend has directed the attention of the House appeared as the heading of the draft which was sent by the United States government to the Canadian government for consideration. This heading was in the following words:
Convention between the United States of America and Great Britain concerning halibut fishery.
When the draft was presented in that form our government'took the view that the convention was not between the United States of America and Great Britain, but between the United States and the Dominion of Canada. Great Britain does not covenant to do anything by this convention. It would have been quite as appropriate and accurate to have stated that the convention was between the United States and South Africa, or New Zealand, or Australia, or Ireland or any other part of the Empire, as it was to say that it was between the American government and Great Britain. Had the American government wished to make reference to the British Empire as a whole the term "British Empire" might have been used. But the entire treaty has relation to the question of fisheries on the Pacific coast of the United States of America and of Canada, and the convention in that respect was therefore one between the United States and Canada. I might point out that the present government was not the only government that drew attention to the apparent error which had been committed in that regard. The British government were kept in touch with the negotiations and were asked for an expression of view on any phase of the proposed agreement. I will read the following telegram which was sent from His grace the Duke of Devonshire, the Secretary of State for the Colonies in Great Britain, to his Excellency, the Governor General. It is dated London, February 15, 1923:
Your telegram January 16th and your despatch January 24th,
Full powers for Mr. Lapointe sent by mail February 13th.
As regards text of draft treaty, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs suggests following modifications:
(1)	Title of treaty to be Convention for the Regulation of Halibut Fisheries on the Paciiio Coast of Canada and the United States.
That is the title the British government suggested should be given to the convention between the two countries.
(2)	In accordance with the usual treaty practice title of his Majesty preamble to read "His Majesty the King of the Urtited Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and the British Dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India."
Do your ministers see any objection?
It will be observed that the British government itself recognised that the convention related solely to Canada and the United 'States, and was careful in suggesting an appropriate designation to bring in the names of these two countries, making no reference to Great Britain or to any other part of the British Empire. Why does my right hon.
Halibut Fishery Treaty

friend not take exception, to the British government having ventured to make specific reference to Canada?
My right hon. friend had a word to say about preserving the historic form of the execution of treaties. I think I have already pointed out wherein the present government has sought to preserve what has come to be the accepted form in the making, signing and ratifying of treaties affecting different parts of the British Empire. The leader of the opposition suggested there had been some discourtesy; that the British Ambassador at Washington had been overlooked. I will not take up the time of the House to read the entire correspondence, but if anyone will peruse the communications that passed between the several governments he will observe our government was most careful to point out that it was as respects Canada that the signature of the Minister of Marine was desired. We were careful to point out that the treaty had to do entirely with a matter of concern to Canada and its neighbour to the south. We did not at any point say that the British government might not, if it thought desirable, ask the British Ambassador at Washington to sign. We did not say that we would take exception to his signing. What we did do was to point out that, the treaty relating as it did to Canada and the United States exclusively, it was not necessary, in our opinion, that more than the signature of our own minister, who had been given full powers by his Majesty the King, should appear on the agreement I might quote a paragraph from the communication referred to by my right hon. friend, which was despatched on February 28, from His Excellency the Governor General to the Secretary of State for the Colonies:
My ministers are of opinion that, as respects Canada, the signature of the treaty by Mr. Lapointe alone should be sufficient.
And elsewhere;
The view of my ministers, however, is that the treaty being one of concern solely to Canada and the United States, and not affecting in any particular any imperial interests, the signature of the Canadian minister would be sufficient, and they would respectfully request that his Majesty's Ambassador at Washington be instructed accordingly.
What does that language mean? It means by implication that had any Imperial interests been concerned Canada would have expected the British Ambassador as well as her own minister to sign the agreement. But inasmuch as the treaty related exclusively to a Canadian matter, inasmuch as it had no bearing of an Imperial character, we felt it was unnecessary in the circumstances that the British Ambassador should place his

signature beside that of the minister who had negotiated the treaty.

Was there any imperial
interest affecting the French treaty that does not affect this one?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Every treaty
has, I think, to be considered in the light of the circumstances under which it is negotiated, and of which proper and full account should be taken. In negotiating the commercial treaty with France, the Canadian ministers, I think, used to a considerable extent the good offices1 of the British Ambassador at Paris. They were in a foreign European country, the British Ambassador lent his good offices in furthering the negotiations, and while there was no obligation, whatever, necessitating the signature of the British Ambassador, it seems to me wholly appropriate that under the circumstances he should have been asked by our ministers to join with them in signing the convention.

What does my right
hon. friend mean by "good offices?" What good offices were exercised then that were not similar to those offered in this case? I should like the Prime Minister to be more specific.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think it will
be quite evident that negotiations with the United States, owing to the proximity of Washington and Ottawa, can be conducted by ministers and officials in a way in which it is not possible to carry on negotiations of a diplomatic character between Ottawa and some European capital. As I say, each case must be considered on its own merits.

That is not the point
I am raising at all. One may be verbally negotiated, the other may be written. But what good offices were necessary in the negotiation of the French treaty that were not necessary in these negotiations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think I have answered my right hon. friend. It is not a question of what was necessary, but what in the circumstances was appropriate. I would say in this connection, that in previous negotiations with France, my right hon. friend's minister had associated himself with the British Ambassador in Paris for the purpose of concluding a temporary arrangement, to take the place of which the new agreement was intended. Under such circumstances, I think it was only proper that the British Ambassador should have been associated with the treaty.

Will the Prime Minister not admit that this correspondence shows that the good offices of the British Ambassador were proffered and given in just the same way in connection with this treaty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I will not admit anything of the kind.	The correspondence speaks for itself.

The correspondence
discloses this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wish to enter into a verbal discussion with my right hon. friend at the moment.
As to the "preservation of the historic form [DOT]of execution of a treaty," which is the phrase my right hon. friend uses, without attempting in any way to set forth what in the opinion of the government is the proper recognition to be given different parts of the British Empire in matters of the kind, I should like, speaking for myself personally to quote from an article by Sir Robert Borden which has recently appeared, as expressing, in the paragraph which I am about to read, my own views ns to the present position with respect to treaties of concern to Canada, and the course of action appropriate in respect thereto. In the Yale Review for this month there appears nn article by Sir Robert Borden entitled, "The British Commonwealth of Nations." On page 12 the article contains references which have already been quoted by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe). In a copy of this article which has been sent to me by, I think, Sir Robert Borden himself, I find inserted the page which I have in my hand, with the following note at the head:
The following paragraph was inadvertently omitted by the Yale Review. It should appear on page 12 at the place indicated.
The place indicated is at the end of the sentence quoted by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. This is Sir Robert Borden's view of the present position in the matter of *treaty-making so far as Canada is concerned.
Since the beginning of the present century Canada *has in many instances negotiated treaties that concerned her special interests. In such cases the diplomatic unity of 'the commonwealth is preserved by the form of the treaty and by the method of execution and ratification.
The King is named in the treaty as the High Contracting Party and the execution is undter powers issued by him upon the recommendation of the Dominion government. Ratification takes place also upon the recomendation of the Dominion government; but any relevant question as to the effect of the treaty upon the commonwealth as a whole must naturally be the subject of consultation between the governments concerned prior to ratification. It is not improbable that in this respect usage, arising out
of practice and experience as to the proper character, method and extent of such consultation, will develop into a recognized convention. There seems no reason to desire or to anticipate any modification in the form of such treaties. The ancient formula by which the King is designated as the enacting authority still subsists in the statutes of each dominion and in those of Great Britain; in form the King, in reality the legislature, enacts.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let me direct attention to these words, " The king is named in the treaty as the high contracting party." That is precisely what we have in the treaty which the House is now considering. The treaty is between His Majesty the King, and the United States. "Its execution is under powers issued by him upon the recommendation of the Dominion government." There appears in the correspondence which lies on the Table of the House a copy of the order in council under which the Dominion government asked His Majesty the King to give full powers to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to act in his name in the negotiating and signing of this treaty The government in so doing acted with a full sense of its responsibility to this parliament. The power rests here with parliament. It is this parliament that in reality is enacting this treaty. It is enacting the treaty through the recommendation made by the ministry in office to-day, which is responsible to parliament, and which has made its recommendation to the king, which recommendation the king has accepted and on which action has been taken.
The Prime Minister had better be a little more accurate in that regard. Does he wish to convey the impression that the king acted upon the advice of this government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think I am perfectly accurate, Mr. Speaker. I say the king's action in this regard was based upon the recommendation of this government.

The Prime Minister did not say so. It was the commencement of the negotiations that led to the king's action. But the advice tendered His Majesty to act would be the advice of the British government, of his own ministers, and this government communicated, not with His Majesty, but with the British government and got it to give that advice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend is resorting to the kind of hair-splitting of which he is so fond.

No, this is very important.
Halibut Fishery Treaty

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The essential thing so far as this parliament and country is concerned is that this govsrr.ment made a certain recommendation to the king. It may be asked: How that recommendation was transmitted, and in what form it was sent? It was sent to His Majesty's ministers in Great Britain and transmitted by them to the King.
With their advice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I am prepared to say, "with their advice." Which shows that they approved entirely of the action to which my right hon. friend now takes exception.
No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend is taking exception to the fact that the Canadian minister signed this treaty.

No, I am not, and I will not permit the Prime Minister to misrepresent me. I object to no such thing. Nor did I object to the recommendation made to the British government for transmission to His Majesty with their advice. It is the proper method. I entirely approve of it, and I entirely approve of the appointment of the Canadian minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Then what is my right hon. friend objecting to?
What I did object to was the change in the usual practice and the refusal by this government to permit the British Ambassador to be associated in the execution of the treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think, Mr. Speaker, I have made it plain that the usual practice, at least in the view of the one member of the Privy Council who has the largest experience, is that as respects matters affecting Canada, a Canadian minister should sign on behalf of His Majesty and be given full power for that purpose, That practice was established by the conference at Versailles and by the Disarmament Conference at Washington.
Will the Prime Minister give me an instance where the British ministers did not sign as well?
They did not sign the Peace Treaty on behalf of Canada.
I did not say for Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Those were
matters of general and Imperial interest in which all parts of the Empire were concerned.
The French treaty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The present
treaty is not a matter which is of imperial interest; it is primarily of concern to this country.

Will the Prime Minister permit an interruption, not a question? He says they were matters of general and imperial interest; surely he does not mean that. I do not wish to be always harping on the Frenoh treaty, but will he say that that treaty is of more imperial interest than this? Or the Italian and other treaties? Or the treaty negotiated four years ago with France? All those are as distinctly Canadian as this one. I wish the Prime Minister would not make such general remarks without being careful as to their real significance.
That is a question.

I do not say it is a
question.
Well, it is a lecture.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I know my right hon. friend is a little restive. He realizes the position he is in, and is simply trying to extricate himself as best he can.
No, not at all. Try to be fair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am prepared to leave it at that. So far as the government's action in this matter is concerned, far from there being any desire or intention in any way to overlook the British Ambassador, the chief and sole aim was to preserve the recognition of the status of Canada as one of the self-governing dominions of the Empire and those full rights of autonomy and responsibility which she has acquired and which during recent years have been so often referred to by her public men.
I shall conclude with one further reference to a remark of my right hon. friend. He said that he could not understand why there was this desire-and he applied his words to this treaty-"to dissociate ourselves from the British Empire." I think I am quoting my right hon. friend correctly in that remark.
I am not quite sure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am very glad my right hon. friend is not quite sure, because I regard his remark as thoroughly disloyal, I marvel at any leader of any party in this House venturing to say that the government was seeking to dissociate itself from the British Empire.

Halibut Fishery Treaty

I did not say anything of the sort. The Prime Minister is imagining it in order to get an excuse to work up his heat. If the Prime Minister will take my remarks as they appear in the typewritten transcript of Hansard, and will wait until eight-thirty tonight, I shall be prepared to stand by the report of what I said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have the very words of my right hon. friend. I quote his words as I took them down. He said he could not understand why there was "this desire to dissociate ourselves from the British Empire." That is the sort of expression my right hon. friend is fond of using when he does not think he will be brought to book for it. I tell my right hon. friend that the government, in the action it was taking, far from being prompted by a desire in any way to estrange Canada from the Empire, believed that its action was calculated to strengthen the faith of Canadians in the greatness of the Empire, and to increase the respect which all other parts of the Empire and other countries have for Canada.
I wish to quote again words of Sir Robert Borden from the article to which I have referred. At page 15, Sir Robert says:
I am of those who believe that the essential unity of the commonwealth has in no sense been diminished by its development into an organization which is virtually a Britannic League of Nations.
That at all events is the position which we on this side of the House take. We believe that the more the British Empire comes to be understood as a Britannic League of Nations, the more serviceable it will be to its component parts and to human society in general, and the more likely will it be to endure on a permanent basis. It is as a part of a league of Britannic nations, as one of a community of sister nations within the British Empire, that we have taken a course which we believe will afford recognition to that particular status. There never has been a time when the assertion of her autonomy by Canada has not been followed by some protest from one quarter or another. We believe that the more self-government is realized in all its phases, the more enduring and permanent will be the basis of the Empire.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, I am one who believes strongly in that community of free nations which comprises the British Empire, and I hope to live to see that community of nations grow stronger from year to year, and as time goes on to mean more and more to our great human society. I believe that in the British commonwealth to-day, we have the greatest example the world has ever
known of a community of free nations in the nature of a League of Nations which is an inspiration and a model to the League of Nations itself. As the British Empire endures so will the League of Nations prosper on similar foundations of liberty and freedom, and consultation and co-operation between component parts. It is because I want to see the British Empire endure, it is because I want to see all its parts work together in closer harmony and co-operation-because I believe it is the greatest agency which the world has ever had for the preservation of freedom, liberty and justice-that I hope every effort will be made upon the part of each free nation of the British Empire to see that in the matter of self-government, it exercises to the full the rights which are conceded to it, as being a component part of the Empire. In that way it will help to illustrate and make for that freedom, justice and cooperation among the nations of the world which we pray all may come to practise and enjoy.
I shall conclude with but one further quotation. On the 24th of May, His Majesty, the King, addressed a message to the school children in all parts of the British Empire. Here are the words with which His Majesty concluded that address. They have been recorded in all the schools of the Empire:
Get knowledge, be brave, honourable and kind, thinking of others before yourselves, and always play the game. So will you fit yourselves to hand down this community of free nations to your children and grandchildren as a great instrument for justice, peace and goodwill, which will deserve the respect and esteem of mankind.
I submit Sir, that we will not find anywhere a truer and nobler expression of what the British Empire is than in those words of His Majesty, wherein he speaks of it as a "community of free nations." If we are a community of free nations, is it to be said as my hon. friend, the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), has suggested with respect to the signing of a treaty affecting Canada but not affecting any imperial interest, that there is no question as to the right you have; you have the right but you must not exercise it? Mr. Speaker, we have passed that stage. We want not only the right, we want also to exercise our rights. We believe that in the exercise of all our rights we will gain more of strength and of influence as a nation; and, so far as the British Empire is concerned, we believe that its greatness will be proportionately greater as our strength and influence as a country increase.

Motion agreed to.

After Recess

-CLOSE SEASON FIXED FOR CANADIAN TERRITORIAL WATERS
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure for the protection of the Northern Pacific halibut fishery, and to provide:
1.	That a close season be established during which it shall be unlawful for any person to fish for, catch or attempt to catch halibut in the territorial waters of Canada contiguous to the western coast of Canada, or for any national or inhabitant of Canada to fish for, catch or attempt to catch halibut in the territorial waters of Canada aforesaid, in the territorial waters of the United States contiguous to the western coast of the United States, in the high seas extending west-terly from the limit of the territorial waters of Canada and of the United States, also Behring Sea.
2.	That making use of a Canadian port to outfit a vessel to engage in prohibited fishing, or permitting the departure of the same with intention to engage in such fishing, or entering any port in Canada while prosecuting a voyage to fish for halibut or with halibut intentionally caught in the close season, shall be an offence against the proposed legislation.
3.	That the vessel, cargo and outfit operated or used for the purpose of committing an offence against the provisions of the proposed legislation shall be liable to seizure and forfeiture, and if such vessel is the property of a national or inhabitant of the United States or is registered in the United States the same shall be delivered as soon as practicable after seizure to an authorized official of the United States to be dealt with in accordance with the laws of that country.
4.	That foreign ships found fishing or preparing to fish for halibut in such territorial waters shall be liable to seizure and to be forfeited, and that certain

provisions of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act be made applicable for the purposes of the proposed legislation.
5.	That the Governor in Council may join with the government of the United States in appointing an International Fisheries Commission, consisting of four members, two to be appointed by the Governor in Council and two by the government of the United States, such commission to exist for a period of five years, and thereafter until two years from the day when either of the constituting governments shall give notice of desire to terminate it, and Canada shall pay the salaries and expenses of the members of the commission appointed by the Governor in Council, and one-half the joint expenses incurred by the commission.
6.	That the Governor in Council may make regulations for giving effect to the recommendations of the commission, and to give full effect to the provisions of the proposed act, and such regulations may create offences and impose penalties, and that the said act shall come into force on a day to be named by the Governor in Council, and may be repealed by the Governor in Council at any time during the existence of the International Fisheries Commission.
Motion, agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On paragraph 1.

This is the general clause of the resolution. I do not wish to take the occasion to make any particular speech but to correct some misrepresentations of the speech I made, if you call it a speech, on the motion itself. I did not realize that I had committed such a grave attack or propounded some new and dangerous theory affecting our autonomy such as called for the long volley of reply that came from lion, gentlemen opposite. I did not know that my innocent remarks were really worthy of a whole afternoon of thunder from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), from the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Morin), and finally from the Prime Minister.
I have not any accusation of misrepresentation, certainly not of deliberate misrepresentation, to make against the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I think that so far as he referred to my own remarks he was quite fair. All I have to say about his reference to them is this:	He seemed to assume,
and he seemed sincerely to assume, that my objection was to the fulness of Canadian autonomy and the fulness of Canadian national rights, that I harboured in my heart the idea that domination from Britain would be advisable. No one in this country would resist the going into effect of any such theory or idea more determinedly than would I. The thought of domination

has long since ceased to be in the mind of any practical person or any prominent person in public affairs in either Britain or Canada. Hear, hear. Could I receive a better confirmation of what I have stated? Already it is declared by the "hear, hears" that I have delivered such a speech this afternoon.
Hear, hear.

Now I place myself in
tke hands of the House. Is my hon. friend

Le Canada.
