Hear, hear. That is
what I thought too.

The modest views of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries agree with my own. With those quotations enunciated I have no quarrel whatever; with some of them I had to do at the time of their creation, but I am no more loyal to them than . I am to the others. I do not know any at this day who disagree. Nothing was said this afternoon on the part of any hon. member in this House out of accord with what was quoted by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, unless it was certain phrases that fell,
I hope inadvertently from the lips of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Morin). Something has been achieved all right through these years, not against obstacles at all but simply as a matter of natural growth. Something has been achieved in that way of fuller national status for our country, fuller control over local affairs, fuller influence over those wider affairs that more and more affect us as we grow in stature and in consequence. I say again it has not been achieved against resistance. I have not witnessed nor come in contact with any resistance on the part of British statesmen or the British people- none whatever. But control of our own affairs, and increasing influence in other matters in which we are interested are quite consistent with the preservation of that co-operation and that unity upon which, at least, as much depends as upon the preservation of our autonomy.
I argued this afternoon against what I deemed an indecorous casting aside of one evidence of that unity without any purpose being served whatever, without any object being gained; nothing whatever being achieved in the way of control of domestic affairs or of control of our part in any affairs at all. Without anything to be gained I do not think it is worth while.
Now, I go further than I went this afternoon. I think his conduct has been a grave mistake, and I will tell the Minister of Marine and Fisheries why. In the conduct of our diplomatic affairs-using the adjective for want of a better-in the conduct of our treaty and other relations with other powers and nations of the world, it is essential, so long as the British Empire exists-whether you call it a commonwealth of nations or the British Empire; one title is as good to me as another, but the latter carries with it a tradition that I for one am not going to forget- it is going to be essential that in all these relations there shall exist harmony and a unity of purpose; in a word that
Halibut Fishery

all our outside relations are harmonized so that we present to the world not a discordant but a united front. I do not mean by this a hostile front but that we present to the world the fact that we are still together, and that we are not one of us pursuing a policy which conflicts and discords with the policy of the other. The means we have adopted in the past of doing so have been to associate with us in the maintenance of our outside relations the appropriate representative of the British government; and by means of such association we take care that we are not entering into covenants or commitments at variance with policies which, although they may be general, though they may be of British rather than Canadian origin, are nevertheless of consequence to us the same as they are of consequence to Britain. Such association we have always preserved, and I want to know what the reason is for not having the preservation of that association attested by the signature of the British representative? Would it not be better in later times, if anything should arise which would make it appear that we possibly had given cause for embarrassment in connection with other affairs to the British Empire, to be able to point to the signature of the British representative as attesting not only consent or approval, but rather attesting the fact that there is nothing within the four corners of the treaty that is in any way detrimental or embarrassing to other interests of the Empire?
Does my right lion, friend mean thereby that a few matters concerning Canada alone should at all times receive the rubber stamp of the British Ambassador?

I was not referring to rubber stamps at all. Matters concerning Canada alone, purely domestic matters never have; but in the case of matters affecting the relations of this country with other countries it is better to have the attestation of a representative of Britain; because though they may appear-and though doubtless they often are-what one may call the sole concern of the Dominion it is not for us alone to say that such is the case. There may be others concerned, although, perhaps, not nearly so much concerned as we are; there may be other relations affected besides our own. Can we stand up and say to all the rest of this Empire "This is our concern and our concern alone" when the matter affects relations with an outside nation? If this is to be done hon. gentlemen say we still preserve unity? I do not know just what hon. genlemen are willing to preserve. What is there left to preserve if we are to make-as stated for example by

the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville -what treaties we like, or as he expressed it, make treaties between the Dominion of Canada and foreign nations in absolute diplomatic freedom, to use his exact words. If we act in this way I ask again, what is there left to preserve? You may preserve a feeling. But a feeling may exist between any other country and the United Kingdom but, in a word what is there to preserve if there is not diplomatic unity to preserve.

Does my right hon. friend intend to start the debate over again? This is entirely out of order. I do not want to interrupt my right hon. friend but the treaty has been approved. Discussion of the signature to that treaty has nothing to do with the legislation now before the House. There is no question of the treaty in this legislation. We are asking merely the right to close our ports and impose penalties in the case of persons fishing in our territorial waters.

I know that I have not
the right to start the debate over again, and I do not intend to. The extent to which I have gone is attributable in part to questions put and interruptions made. I will not proceed any further. I wanted to make my position on the subject clear. I will not start in to refute or attempt to destroy what has been said on the other side. I will make no reference to the alleged reply of the Prime Minister, inasmuch as from beginning to end it was based on a distortion of my own remarks.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 2.

I would like to have the minister's views as to the validity of the proposed law in regard to extra-territorial rights. The committee will remember that this House passed an address two or three years ago, asking that there should be an amendment to the British North America Act giving this country the same power of legislation in personam, but in relation to extra-territorial rights or extra-territorial offences, that the British government itself possesses in relation to their own subjects. Certain objections were taken to it, but it passed this House anyway, and was forwarded, and I am not quite certain'-I cannot recall definitely-as to the reasons why it has not yet been adopted; but until it is adopted, how have we the right to legislate even in personam? The minister understands me.

Yes.

Halibut Fishery

The minister knows we
have not the right to legislate as to what might be done by others than the citizens of Canada in extra-territorial waters. That is to say, if the offence is committed in extraterritorial waters, how can we legislate against it in the absence of an amendment to the British North America Act?

I quite understand the
objection. I was not absolutely sure about it; but it was referred to the Department of Justice, and the resolution and the bill have been drafted by that department. Of course, where other people are concerned, there is no doubt we would have no right in extraterritorial waters; but it seems the Justice department are of the opinion that we can deal with Canadian citizens in those waters.

It is the only way, of
course, in which we can meet the obligations under the treaty, but I am inclined to think the Justice department is taking a flyer at it -taking the chance. I suppose it cannot do any harm.

Perhaps my hon. friend has the opinion of the Department of Justice. Certainly the Department of Justice once upon a time had a very different view. This House adopted the resolution it did adopt as a result of the opinion of the Department of Justice. The question then arose having particular regard to aeroplanes. We became interested in offences by Canadian citizens outside of our territorial jurisdiction, and the opinion of the Department of Justice then certainly was that we had no right to create an offence, whether by a Canadian citizen or anybody else, outside territorial waters. That is why they adopted that resolution. What new light has the department got?

If the offence is committed
on the high seas, who has the right? Surely some one has.

The hon. member has not quite got the drift of this question at all. The Mother Country has the territorial rights. We have all rights given us in connection with our own land. Those rights extend to the three-mile limit. What we wanted to do-and the reason this resolution was passed before-was to put ourselves in the position of being able to police these districts. Take the case of the aeroplane. Of course the law is different in reference to ships. We need not worry about that question. We wanted the right to be able to police outside the three-mile limit.

Does the hon. membpn
mean to say that Canada has no control over Canadian citizens on the high seas?

No, that is the whole thing; and the House adopted the resolution that we should have an amendment to the British North America Act which would give us extra territorial rights? The whole House, on the advice of the Department of Justice, was told that we had not that control. I understand my hon. friend to say to-day that the Justice department has changed its mind. I think the best way of showing how it has changed its mind would be to read its opinion. I know of nothing i hat has turned up in the meantime to make a change.

In answer to my hon. friend's question, the Justice department prepared the legislation. We asked the Justice department to prepare the legislation to meet the requirements of the treaty, and to prepare if, of course, according to our laws, and this is the bill and the resolution which were prepared, not by us, but by the Department of Justice.

But the instructions to the department in that case would be just the same as in any other matter. Here is a treaty; we want an act to carry it into effect and provide for it, and among other matters, we have this question. Did the minister get an opinion from the department whether that bill if enacted would bo the law?
We had the opinion of the Department of Justice before the bill was prepared.

The Department of Justice would never vouch that this clause would be effective. It is put there, in the hope that people would follow it, and not in the belief ihat we have the jurisdiction to pass it.
I do not admit that.
They gave a previous opinion to that effect.
I am bound by the fact that they have presented the bill.
Does the minister say the department has expressed the opinion that this House has jurisdiction to give effect to penalties for violation of these provisions?

I say the Department o! Justice prepared the bill to meet what is contemplated by the treaty. They made a difference, as my right hon. friend will see when
Halibut Fishery

he has the bill, in section 2, as between the citizens of Canada and foreign citizens. In reference to territorial waters, it applies to everybody from everywhere. In extra-territorial waters it applies only to citizens of Canada, because we are supposed to have thr-i'ght to prohibit only Canadian citizens in extra-territorial waters. They did this and prepared this legislation; they were asked by the Department of Marine and Fisheries to prepare legislation according to the law.

And the Justice department-poor fellows-what else could they do? Here is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries bound by that treaty to give effect to certain things, one of which the government of Canada was not in position to give effect to. That is handed to the Justice department and they are asked to prepare a law to do that. They prepare this, and it is the best they could do. Certainly I could not have done it better if I had been asked to do it. But the Justice department will not say that we have power to give effect to it.
My hon. friend knows that the Justice department would never lend itself to the preparation of a law which it knew to be illegal or to be one that could not be enforced.
I do not know; they might have to. What else could they do?
I am not a dictator to the Department of Justice.

It would be the duty of the Department of Justice to prepare a law to carry the treaty into effect. It is not their fault if we have not the power to give effect to that treaty; it is the fault of those who made the treaty. There are cases, which I shall not mention because I am not familiar with them, where the same thing has had to be done on other occasions; but on this occasion they could only do what they have done. The minister got them into that position.
No.
Oh, yes; and now he is making a treaty which in my opinion, as, I am sure, in the opinion of the Justice department as well, this country has no power to carry through.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 4.

Suppose the ships of some foreign country, say, Japan, come into extraterritorial waters off the Canadian coast, there

would be no power to prevent them from fishing?
No.

In that case does the
treaty purpose to restrain the nationals of Canada and of the United States from fishing, while permitting foreign vessels to engage in the business?
As I explained this afternoon, it is impracticable for foreign vessels tc come and fish off the coast without using our ports, and that we can prevent them from doing.
I heard the minister say that but I do not agree with him.
Well you are wrong.
I know a little about this matter.
And so do other people.

The reason the Japanese do not fish halibut off the Pacific coast is that the market for this fish is in the New England states, in eastern Canada and elsewhere in America. There is a very small market for that class of fish in the Orient, where they get the cheaper fish. But within the last five years the Japanese have gone into the salmon canning business and have virtually put British Columbia and Alaska salmon off the British market. This appeared in a government report the other day and is also recorded in public statements. I apprehend that as soon as this restriction is imposed on the nationals of Canada and of the United States the Japanese will make efforts to find a market for this particular fish, because there is no difficulty in their coming across, fishing off the coast, icing the fish and taking it back to the Orient. The only trouble in their way at present is the lack of a market for this high-class fish. My hon. friend comforts himself with the thought that they cannot come and fish.
I have the advice of experts on the subject.

The opinion of many to whom I have spoken, and my opinion also, is that they will come as soon as they find a market for this fish; and I expect that to occur in a few years' time. I suggest that we should be prepared in such an eventuality to know exactly what we are going to do.

Then my hon. friend is
opposed to the close season.

Halibut Fishery
No, no. The minister is misinterpreting my remarks.

There is no way of preventing Japanese vessels from coming and fishing off the coast if they can do so without using either our ports or the American ports. If they can come and fish under such circumstances we are unable to prevent them. Nevertheless, everybody in my hon. friend's province is asking for this legislation because it is highly important that there shall be a close season if the halibut, which are being destroyed in alarming numbers, are to be conserved. We have had representations from every source in British Columbia, and I have not heard one word against this proposed legislation and the treaty. We cannot meet the difficulty in any other way.
I am not for one moment suggesting that this legislation should not be passed. I merely want to know what we are going to do should foreign vessels come and fish during the close season.

I have already pointed out that there is no means by which we can prevent them from coming and fishing. Perhaps my hon. friend can suggest one. We have no right to go into extra-territorial waters and stop anybody who wants to fish. If we had a treaty with the Japanese we might be able to do so, but we have not. But the advice of all experts on this subject convinces us that neither Japanese
9 p.m. nor any other foreign vessels can carry on fishing operations in these waters which are covered by the treaty. In the extra-territorial waters our restrictions can apply only to our own citizens; similarly the American government will control its own nationals. But we believe that it is imperative that we should prevent our citizens from carrying on operations, and should make .t impossible for foreigners to do the same, by closing our ports. That is the only way we can save the industry; otherwise we should have to let the halibut disappear in a very short time.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 5.
When are the commissioners to be appointed?

When the treaty has
come into force, after its ratification. They will not be appointed before next winter.
Not before ratification by the United States?

No.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Lapointe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 247 for the protection of the Northern Pacific Halibut Fishery.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Mr. LAPOINTE moved the second reading of the bill.
Motion agreed to and the House went into-committee on the bill, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 2-Interpretation.

I notice that paragraph (d) of clause 2 provides that the prohibited waters shall comprise certain waters in Canada and off the United States shore, and also the Behring sea. Why is the Behring sea included in this? It must be remembered that the Japanese, for instance, have far easier access to the Behring sea than our fishermen have.
As I said this afternoon, the treaty was drafted by the United States themselves. We were asked to include the Behring sea and I do not see any objection to doing so.

I am not in a position, perhaps, to offer any facts to back up what I am going to suggest; it may be that our interests there are nil. But it would appear to me as if we were legislating ourselves out of any right to enter the Behring sea, and that is not necessary for the purposes of this treaty. It must be remembered that one has to go away round the Aleutian islands, a couple of thousand miles or more from Prince Rupert, to approach the Behring sea, which is not near the halibut fisheries at all.
What will be the harm in including it if it is not near the halibut fisheries?
I cannot tell my hon. friend what the harm is unless he can tell me why it is in here. To me it is a purposeless thing, unless the United States government had some reason for putting it there.

I do not think myself that it serves a very important purpose, but I would not like to add a rider or reservation to the treaty to exclude the Behring sea. As my hon. friend himself says, the inclusion of the words "Behring sea" cannot have any effect, because there are no halibut there.

What I meant was this: The present halibut fisheries, so described, lie off the Queen Charlotte islands and the panhandle of Alaska, the southern narrow strip
Halibut Fishery

of the Alaskan coast running down the British Columbian coast. Up to the present the halibut fishing in the Behring sea has not been developed, but I am not so positive that there are no halibut there; it looks as if some information that we are not possessed of induced the American government to include the Behring sea in the treaty. It will certainly give a distinct advantage to the Japanese. If there is any need for including the Behring sea, in the absence of any other information we must assume there are halibut there, and if that is the case the Japanese will have access to those fisheries while we have not.

My hon. friend may be sure that neither the United States nor Canada have entered into this treaty and have included the Behring sea for the benefit of the Japanese. I do not think the United States are trying to facilitate matters for the Japanese and to enable them to fish in their waters, any more than we are doing in our own waters. This is an honest effort to provide a close season and to prevent American and Canadian fishermen from destroying the halibut. Both countries have for years been trying to arrange this close season and the treaty has been drafted in such a way as to cover all possibility of fishing in violation of this close season.
Virtually the minister's answer to my question is that he does not know why the Behring sea is included.
Just to make sure that we shall have a close season wherever there is a possibility of halibut fishing being carried on.

Is there not a danger in including the Behring sea? On the Atlantic I would not see very much danger so far as the extra-territorial waters are concerned, but in Behring sea you are very close to Japan, which is a fishing nation. Is not the ultimate effect just going to be to make the Behring sea a fishing preserve for the good of Japan alone? The minister says the United States would never do that. Well, what is the good of this parliament ratifying the treaty if we are only going to be able to plead in defence of our wisdom that we are relying on the good sense of the United States? We had better just refer the matter to the United States senate and tell them to act for Canada. We ourselves would like to know in ratifying this treaty what it is going to do for us. The minister says the inclusion of Behring sea will not do any harm. It looks to me as if it would; it looks to me as if it would

shut Canadians out should they be disposed to go up there, and make of Behring sea a sort of reserve for Japan.
My hon. friend may be sure there is no idea of making it a reserve for Japan.
Is that not the effect?

This treaty has been carefully considered by the officers of the fisheries departments of both the United States and Canada. It is the result of their combined investigations and of what they know of the fishery conditions in these various waters, and they thought that Behring sea should be included. We cannot prevent the Japanese from going there; there is no doubt about that, but we want to have a close season in as considerable an area as possible.

I cannot conceive of any possible reason for including Behring sea if it is the object to preserve the halibut fisheries of the Pacific coast. Furthermore, if a reason does exist, then we are simply abandoning the Behring sea to the Japanese. That is the effect of this legislation.

If that is the effect, my hon. friend may be sure that both Canada and the United States will be willing to amend the legislation so as to exclude the Behring
sea.
I have no doubt that is correct, but it is a remarkable plea to make in defence of a treaty.
I do not admit that that would be the effect.

I know the minister does not admit it, but this is his argument: I cannot see what good the inclusion of these words is going to do; I cannot see why it should not perhaps do harm, but if it turns out that way we shall be willing to amend the treaty.	.
Those are not exactly my words. The middle part of my right hon. friend's remarks is from his own lips.
It is simply a plainer statement of what my hon. friend has just said.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Knowingly in possession of halibut unlawfully caught.

I want to point out again to the minister a possible effect of this. We have not developed on the Pacific coast the

Halibut Fishery
trawler system of fishing to any considerable extent for reasons that may perhaps disappear as time goes on and the country expands. If trawler fishing in the Behring sea is developed; if good fishing grounds are discovered there, Canadian and American vessels catching halibut in their trawls would be forced to comply with this act; the halibut would have to be turned in and sold, and so forth. But the Japanese, fishing right alongside, would have the full privilege of fishing with trawlers and keeping the fish. Within the past five or ten years the Japanese have developed a salmon fishery in the Behring sea which is rapidly displacing the fishing of the Americans and Canadians on the Pacific coast. I merely cite that to illustrate that fishing in that district is in its infancy and that its development under the conditions that I have described wrould result in disaster to us.
My hon. friend knows that the close season is for three months only, during the winter. I do not think there would be any salmon fishing in the Behring sea in the month of January.
I am not talking about salmon fishing; I am talking about halibut fishing.
My hon. friend suggested that while engaged in other fishing the Japanese might catch halibut and would be entitled to keep it. But there is no other fishing there during that close season.

But the Japanese can go in there with trawlers; they can trawl for halibut, and if they discover a halibut bed in the Behring sea they may take the fish and keep them. Does my hon. friend not see the force of that contention? If instead of arguing away from the point the minister would admit that he does not know why the Behring sea is included and that while it is too late to remedy it he would undertake to examine into the matter and if possible get the Americans to exclude the Behring sea, that would be a reasonable answer.

That far I can go,
surely.

It is hardly sufficient to answer that it is not likely to happen. I rather expect that not only in the Behring sea but on the Pacific coast the old beds which we are seeking to preserve will within five years be fished quite extensively by the Japanese.

Section agreed to.
On section 11-International Fisheries Commission.
I have just seen the bill at this moment. I' note that there are to be four commissioners, who are to be empowered to make recommendations concerning regulations.
This is to carry out the recommendation of the International Commission of 1918.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.
Mr. LAPOINTE moved the third reading of the bill.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a clause in this bill has just been drawn to my attention which does seem rather remarkable. Section 13 says:
This act shall come into force on a day to be named by the Governor in Council-
So much for order in council.
-and may be repealed by the Governor in Council,-
So much more for order in council.
-provided that it shall not be repealed by the Governor in Council at any time during the existence of the International Fisheries Commission hereinbefore authorized.
Where is this government going to stop? Why not ask parliament for a bill authorizing it to make treaties with any country at any time of any kind and repeal them at any time and on any occasion? It would save a lot of the time of the House. The government asks for power of unconditional repeal; what is parliament for? If parliament deals with the passing of an act, surely parliament should be asked when the act should be repealed. There is no reason for asking parliament's authority to pass if you give the government unconditional authority to repeal. There have been cases where the power of repeal has been reserved to be exercised on the happening of a certain event named by parliament; thus parliament has the whole say. But here there is no event it all; the government decides when to repeal the act that parliament passes. Where is this order in council policy going to stop? I do not know anything else I could suggest to the government to enable it to take everything into its own hands and away from parliament that it has omitted. This is one art the ministers have mastered, and possibly having mastered something they ought to be left to its exercise.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
There is nothing
very mysterious about this thing.

terious.
It is not mysterious; I It is certainly not mys-It is autocratic.
This close season cannot be enforced until the United States congress ratifies the treaty and until the exchange of ratifications takes place. We cannot have this law in force now-
I do not object to that, but-

Another condition may
arise that would give occasion for the putting of the legislation into force. If the United States government, without the ratification of the treaty by the United States senate, passes similar legislation, enacting exactly the same clauses, the Governor in Council may then put this into force, and that cannot be done otherwise than by order in council.
My hon. friend-

Now, if the right hon.
gentleman will permit me-
If the minister will excuse me, I did not take any exception
I would like to continue if my right hon. friend will allow me.
I do not want the minister to misrepresent me.
I have not misrepresented anybody
He intimated I was objecting to the government having power to call the act into effect. I was not. I objected to the government having power unconditionally to repeal it.

It was not necessary for my hon. friend to interrupt me to say what he has just said. The difference between what this government is doing now and that famous government by order in council to which he referred is this: Parliament knows what we are going to do. We are asking parliament to give us the power to put this law into force if certain conditions arise. My right hon. friend was legislating by order in council. He was inaugurating policies in this country without parliament ever having been consulted on those policies. That is just the difference.
I ask the hon. gentleman now to name one single instance.
Oh!
Already the hon. gentleman is becoming the official jeerer for the government.

No, but my right hon.
friend is something else.

I ask him now to give
one single instance in the ten years when the late government did by order in council anything which it was not authorized to do by the parliament of this country.

If it is quite in order
I am quite willing to answer my right hon. friend. I can give him one specific instance if he wants it.
Yes.

During two consecutive
sessions of parliament the government of my right hon. friend introduced legislation in the House to appoint a purchasing commission. The bill was fought in parliament and the government had to withdraw it. The following session the same thing happened again, and the bill was withdrawn a second time, and then when every member of the House had gone home after the close of the session an order in council was passed instituting the purchasing commission.
He has come to a specific case as he states. I tell the hon. member that the order in council which was passed was entirely within the power of the government.
Oh, oh.
A laugh does not answer. A laugh may be all that is within the power of hon. gentlemen, but it is no answer. Not only so, but the government obtained the opinion of the Justice department.
Read the opinion.

Read it 1 The government obtained the opinion of the Justice department stating that we had the power to pass what we did. We did not pass indeed any order in council establishing a buying commission. We passed an order in council whereby through a commission the government could buy.

I did not say the government had no right to do it. The government had any right under the War Measures Act. They could do anything under that act, and that is what they did in that specific instance.

The hon. gentleman is
wrong there. If it had been passed under

Business Profits War Tax
the War Measures Act, the War Measures Act was passed by parliament and it was legislation of parliament the same as any other legislation. As a matter of fact, it was not passed on the authority of that act at all. The hon. gentleman should be more careful. It was passed under the authority of powers vested in ministers, under the various acts that give the department power. While I am on my feet the Minister of Justice once, not intentionally I know, made the statement last session that every order in council of the late government which had gone before the courts to determine our authority to pass it had been found ultra vires. Not being certain at the time I afterwards went into the matter with the Justice department and reviewed the whole case, and I found that never in the history of the late government was one single order in council which we passed reversed or declared to be illegal by any court.

Unfortunately I have
no right to answer.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend subsection three of section 13 of The Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916, and to remove the restriction of the said subsection by which the liability to pay the tax imposed continues for the period of only three years and by which the minister is permitted at any time within three years only to assess such person for the tax, and to provide that the act shall be construed as if the said restriction had never been contained therein.
Motion agreed to and thfe House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
When the Business
Profits War Tax Act was passed it was evidently treated as a measure of a temporary character. There was a clause in it which reads as follows:
Any person liable to pay the tax shall continue to be so liable for the period of three years from the time at which such tax would have been payable.
The business profits tax has ceased to be operative. No new taxes are being levied under the act, but there is a considerable sum of indebtedness to the government arising from past years, and of course we desire to preserve our right to collect these moneys. There may be some doubt arising from the use of that expression "liable for the period of three years", and we are bring-
286i
ing in this resolution to remove any doubt. The effect of it is that the parties shall be liable. It becomes a debt to the government of Canada to be collected at any time the government are able to collect it.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Without any limitation at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT
speechtext: As to time, certainly. It is like any other debt.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT
speechtext: But unlike any other debt there is no limitation. I do not see why the minister should make it perpetual without any limitation. If the government does not collect say within three years from the date of the assessment, why should the Crown be in any better position than an ordinary creditor?

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Because the Crown is at all times in a better position than a private claimant.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I understand that this will do away with the privilege that obtained in the past of taking notes from certain companies in payment of taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT
speechtext: It does not take away any privilege the government have, but it makes it clear the government have power to collect the debt in any way in which they think they can collect it.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the minister is quite right in bringing down this bill if it is what I assume it is, that is, if it is to remove the limitation of three years and preserve to the Crown its full right of priority to these taxes over all other claims.
