maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL

speechtext:
Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend The Income War Tax Act, 1917, and to provide:
1.	That in any case the income of a tax-payer shall be deemed to be not less than the income from his chief occupation, and if he has income from more than one source the minister shall have power to determine which one or more, or which combination thereof shall, for the purpose of the Act, constitute the tax-payer's chief occupation, and the income therefrom shall be taxed accordingly.
2.	That such reasonable rate of interest on borrowed capital used in the business to earn the income, as the minister in his discretion, may determine, shall be allowed as a deduction, notwithstanding the rate of interest payable by the tax-payer. To the extent that the interest payable by the tax-payer is in excess of the amount allowed by the minister, it shall not be allowed as a deduction.
3.	That in computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed, a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of the disbursements or expenses not wholly, exclusively and necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the income, or any outlay, loss or replacement of capital or any depreciation, depletion or obsolescence, except as otherwise provided in the Act.
4.	That further provisions be made respecting the exemption of the income of Consuls and Consuls General, and of officials or officers of a foreign country, and respecting the exemption of the income of officials of Great Britain or any of its self-governing colonies and of the pensions of any member of the military, naval or air forces of His Majesty's Allies.
5.	That in the case of a return by an employer, the penalty shall be further limited to an amount equal to ten per cent of the aggregate amount of the tax payable by the employees who should be reported on such return, but in any case should the penalty be less than two dollars then in lieu thereof the penalty shall be two dollars.
6.	That sections twelve to twenty-one of the said act be repealed and provisions be made regarding notices of appeal, and for an appeal on notice to the Exchequer Court of Canada from the decision of the minister, and further proceedings thereon.
7.	That all taxes, interest and penalties payable under the act shall constitute a lien upon the assets of the tax-payer, both real and personal, and this lien shall be deemed to attach or to have attached, on the first day of May, immediately succeeding the taxation year in respect of which the tax was payable, or to which the interest and penalties relate, and shall have priority over any mortgage, conveyance or securities as shall be prescribed.
8.	That when the minister has knowledge or suspects that any person is or is about to become indebted to a tax-payer he may demand of such person that the moneys otherwise payable to the tax-payer be in whole or in part paid over to the Receiver General of Canada on account of the tax-payer's liability under this act.
fMr. Fielding.]
9.	That further provisions be made regarding distress in default of payment, and for the recovery of all taxes, interest and penalties in the Exchequer Court of Canada, and for the registration of a certificate of the Commissioner of Taxation as to amounts remaining unpaid, and the enforcement thereof.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I think, as far as these resolutions go, they are likely to have the entire concurrence of the House, and I am inclined to think two or three hon. members would be glad if we' would go much further; but I am cherishing the hope that the resolutions will be found satisfactory. The resolutions do not introduce much that is new. In several instances they are really intended to clarify the existing law. Where a party is engaged in several lines of business, questions arise as to the particular branch of business on which the tax should be levied. It is desirable we should make it clear that whatever is determined to be his chief occupation shall be recognized as the basis of taxation; and as doubts have arisen in that respect, it is made clear here that the minister, in the event of a dispute of that character, shall have the right to determine what is his chief ocupation; and the tax shall be levied accordingly. It is, perhaps, debatable whether we have that power now, but this is designed to make it quite clear.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I think the minister goes a little further. I went through the resolution this afternoon. I think we have had the power always; but the minister is going a little further now. He is providing now that if a man holds two positions, or if he is in two businesses, the minister will have the right to say "both of these are main businesses," and treat them accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: It is giving the minister the power to determine disputes of that character. That is one purpose of the resolution.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Will this section of the act not permit the minister to distinguish what is class A income and what is class B income also?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Yes, it will give the minister-that power.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: In other words, the income will be the sum of the earning capacity of the tax-payer, no matter from what source.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
And also that the tax will be paid on the greatest income the tax-payer has; in other words, if a man's class A income exceeds his class B income, he has to pay on his class A income.

Income Tax

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: That is the old law.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Would the minister inform the committee why no deduction is allowed from class A income, providing the deduction is of a character such as allowed on class B income? In other words, I will illustrate it in this way: the class A income of the taxpayer amounts to $5,000, and the class B income to $2,000. There are deductions allowed under the act with respect to the class B income of $2,500; consequently the deductions, taking a hypothetical case, are more than the man's class B income. The overplus of $500 is not allowed as deductions from class A income; hence the tax-payer is not paying on his net income.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: He is paying on his net income, but he cannot deduct his collateral losses, that is all.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: No, it is not a case of loss at all. It is a question of actual carrying charges. When the income tax came into* effect in 1917, people had many obligations; subsequently, under the administration of the act, and quite correctly so, the income was divided into class A or earned income and class B, unearned income, or income which the man derived from investments which the man had put aside. Unfortunately many people incurred various charges such as mortgages on real estate, interest on borrowed money and so forth, and cases have happened where these charges properly incurred are allowed as deductions from class B income. I should like the minister to explain the theory in the act by which a man does not pay on his net income but pays on the whole of class A income even if he has legal and properly deductable charges from class B income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: There can be no deductions from earned income. Whatever is determined to be the earned income becomes the income of the man's greatest occupation, and from that there can be no deduction.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I hope the minister does
not think me impertinent in pressing the point. If so, I will stop immediately.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend would not be that.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
When the tax-payer's legal deductions under class B income are more than the total of that income, why should not the difference be allowed on account of class A? In other words, why should not the tax-payer pay on his net income? This is a
very important point, because the tax bears very heavily on the people at the present time, particularly on professional men who have a small amount of savings and who, unfortunately, at times have charges which they acquired in past years and which in many cases are more than the whole of their class B income. They struggle along notwithstanding that, but under the income tax law they are not allowed to deduct anything on account of this. They are charged on the whole of their earnings, and I cannot see the justice of that feature of the act.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I hope the minister will
see his way to amend the law in order that the tax may bear less heavily on those who are least able to pay. The income tax to-day is a great hardship on the man with comparatively small earnings and moderate means. It is not a very desirable form of taxation, for it strikes the smaller man at many points; it begins at his breakfast table and is double-edged. If the man has an income of $4,000 he has to pay his municipal tax on the 1st of May in one instalment, and then the federal authorities come along a few days afterwards and tax him a second time. In other words, the small wage earner is taxed to death. The Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, when he brought down his budget on the 5th of February, announced a reduction in the income tax in Great Britain because the country was expecting it. The wage earners in Canada are expecting the same thing, because the present system of taxation is not equitable. In my own city I know of a man who was assessed on $50,000. He represented to the municipal authorities that his income was only $25,000, and they accepted his word and marked it down to that figure. A few days afterwards he took out an insurance policy for several hundred thousand dollars on his business. That instance is well known. But there is no difficulty in the tax collector getting after the small man, and he is hit hardest. There should be some co-ordination of the methods of taxation in this country. In the United States the federal, the state and the municipal authorities agree to allow certain fields of ta/xation to be 10 p.m. exploited exclusively by each of these bodies respectively, and the system has worked out satisfactorily. This tax in Canada has been so onerous that charity is being starved. This is a fact so far as Toronto is concerned. When any business man is appealed to on behalf of the hospitals he declares that his subscription is already paid to the Minister of Finance of the country. The whole basis of taxation in Canada is
Income Tax

wrong. If the war is to be paid for, and nobody suggests that it should not, some method should be found of distributing the burden as equitably as possible so that those who are able will pay more than the less fortunate tax-payers. I hope that next year the minister will provide that incomes up to $4,000, say, shall be exempt from federal taxation. And in the meantime some means ought to be found of co-ordinating the various branches of taxation in this country.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would prefer that I should defer any questions1 I may have to ask until a later stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I do not know that I
can give any particular reason for the law as it exists. It is the law, and I have not been able to change it. I cannot enter into the reasons that actuated those gentlemen who framed the bill.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: The minister has his able assistant with him, but I cannot see where the justice of the law comes in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: The ruling of the department is based on the law, and I am informed that when the act was first introduced the Minister of Finance of that day so explained its purpose. However, the law will have to be judged as it is drawn, and if there is any doubt about the matter the Minister of Justice will be my adviser. The question arises at times respecting interest on borrowed money. It is claimed that the interest on borrowed money in whatever form it may be is a proper charge against a man's business and should be deducted before his income is declared.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: That has always been the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I am informed that it
is doubtful whether the law permits that now. We are proposing to make it clear that where interest is paid in any form in business it is a proper charge against the business and should be deducted before the income is declared.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
The whole
question was as to whether it was borrowed against the business. There is one point, however, on which I would comment. The minister is to fix the rate of interest. Why is that done? Suppose a man has to float a bond at 6 per cent and the annual rate of interest comes to 4 per cent. Is it intended that the actual expenditure which would be 6 per cent will be discounted and cut to 4 per cent? Surely the department should not

interfere with the details of the actual costs of carrying on business.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I may put a case to the
minister. In the year 1921 a company which had made capital commitments prior to that time found themselves in the position of being compelled to borrow money on the market at what proved to be the peak price. Bonds at 8 per cent sold to the underwriters, we will say, at 90, 92 or 95. These bonds ran for a period of twenty years, and can only be callable-I am speaking of industrial institutions-after the stated interval, at a premium. Does the minister propose that as the current rate of interest drops from time to time it shall be allowed as against the income and that the business itself will have to absorb the difference? In the supposititious case I have cited the money cost nearly 110 per cent and the bonds were for a period of twenty years. That was a definite charge against the business as a capital expenditure. It seems to me wholly unfair that in a bona fide case of this character the company shall [DOT] not be allowed to charge the full amount they have to pay. I quite appreciate that the bond discount is another phase of the question, about which I shall have something to say a little later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: The ordinary, reasonable rate of interest would be allowed. But suppose the bonds were issued at a high rate of interest, and produced a premium, that practically is not the real rate of interest at all. I hope my hon. friend sees the point.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: If the bonds are issued at, say, 7 per cent, and are sold at a premium, 7 per cent is not the real interest on that transaction. The object here is to give the minister power to fix a reasonable rate of interest, which would be the ordinary current rate. If under exceptional circumstances a high rate is paid, it would be for the minister to say whether he would allow it or not.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Supposing the 7 per cent bond is sold at a premium of 110, this gives the man 6 per cent money. This presents no difficulty. The whole $110 goes into the business and he is really paying only 6 per cent, although the face of the bond says 7 per cent. If it is a case of fraud, and the money has not gone into the business, the department could look after that under the present law. I really think my hon. friend has not thought this out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
It is an extreme case, but just for illustration suppose the man issues

Income Tax
his 10 per cent bond at 120, he is not paying 10 per cent, and he should not be allowed 10 per cent.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: He would not get it.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: He is being allowed only 10 per cent on 100, not 10 per cent on 120.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: But if the bond is issued at a premium, then you are paying a less rate of interest in reality than appears on the face of the bond.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Surely what he is allowed is the interest he pays, and this is really only 6 per cent on the money he gets. I have every confidence in the minister's adviser in such a matter as this, but either it has been wrongly stated to us or the principle is wrong. As the minister has it to-day, he can make any allowance he likes. He can allow me on what I owe my bank 5 per cent, whereas I may be paying 8. Usually the man whose credit is lowest pays the high rate. According to this, anyone who is in that position is going to have to pay on an income that he really is not getting. In a word, he is going to be penalized for his own poverty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: If he issues 10 per cent bonds at 110, and then claims he is paying 10 per cent and asks for a deduction accordingly, that is certainly not the real rate of interest he is paying.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: But his income tax return does not show what rate he is paying. Supposing he issued a 10 per cent $1,000 bond and sold it for $1,200, he would pay on the $1,000 bond $100, and he would return in his income tax statement the $100 paid. The 10 per cent does not appear at all. That $100 should be allowed. It works out really to be a little more than 8 per cent interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: The bond itself bears 10 per cent as the rate of interest, and he will be tempted to claim 10 per cent, and that is what he would be allowed.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: He cannot.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I am not so sure of that. What we are concerned about is that only a reasonable and fair rate of interest ought to be allowed.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I may be charged more than is fair and reasonable. Hon. gentlemen to my left say that nearly all of their constituents are charged an excessive rate of interest and if they are, and cannot help paying it, it ought to be allowed them. Why should the minister be empowered to .say: Here is a farmer paying 9 per cent, but we
are going to allow him 6 per cent when he puts in his tax papers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: In the case cited of a farmer paying the ordinary rate of interest in his district, this would be a reasonable rate.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Why should the minister have any jurisdiction? A man is not going to pay any higher interest than he can help.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: In the illustration I gave a man may claim he is paying 10 per cent because he pays that on the bond. Of course, that is only an illustration. I do not see any objection so long as the rate of interest to be credited is fair and reasonable.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Suppose he sells his 10 per cent bond at a premium of 25 per. cent, he -would get in cash $125. As against this sum which has gone into the business there is only a charge of $100. His interest payments, although 10 per cent on the face of the bond, are really only 7i per cent on the actual money that is in the business. It would be just exactly the same, assuming that 7i per cent was the proper rate, if he issued a 7i per cent bond and sold it at par. The only room for fraud would be if the man sold his 10 per cent bond at a premium of 25 per cent and put only the $100 in his business, pocketing the $25. Then I would quite agree with my hon. friend, because the man is not paying interest for it. But that is something which could be checked to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: As a matter of fact, he could put that $25 anywhere he likes, but I am advised that according to the law and practice that $25 is not taxable and we do not get the benefit. If he sells at a premium a $1,000 bond bearing interest at 10 per cent he will claim that that is the rate of interest he is paying. Should he in such a case be credited with paying 10 per cent?

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Very well, then this law will say he is not.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Take the illustration advanced by the minister himself of a $100 bond sold at $120 bearing 10 per cent interest. As a matter of fact that means interest at 8 1/3 per cent. If the man puts the $20 premium in his pocket, he must show that as a return in his own personal income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I am informed that that is not the custom.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Then it is a fraud. On the other hand, if he turns it into the busi-
Income Tax

ness, it stands there as part of his capital and ought to be allowed the full interest charged.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I am told that according to the practice of the department, the $25, or whatever the amount, is not taxable. I repeat the case: A man says, "I am paying interest at 10 per cent," and he asks to be allowed that. Under this law he would be told, "No, that is not fair because you do not really pay 10 per cent, you pay 7 or 8 per cent, and we charge you that rate." What is unfair in that?

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Let me put a concrete case to the minister which came under my own personal observation. In 1921 -when money was at a peak price and people had to take care of commitments made prior to the depression, they were obliged to go out and borrow in the market at 8 per cent par. Bonds were sold to underwriters at less than par and were put on the market at one point below par so that the money actually netted the investor 8.10 per cent. Three years later money eases away and is worth only 6 per cent, and these same bonds are quoted at that rate. As I understand it, the purpose of the resolution is to give the minister power to allow only the payment at the rate of 6 per cent on that money, although as a matter of fact the borrower is paying over $160,000 a year interest on the $2,000,000 borrowed. This gives the minister power to allow only S120,000. That is not fair; it is not just.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
In the case my hon.
friend mentions there would be no difficulty whatever. The man is actually paying 8 per cent or a fraction more; under the circumstances that would be a fair and reasonable rate and would be allowed.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
That is not what the
resolution says.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: So far as giving the minister power is concerned, I am not anxious to have that power; if it could be exercised by somebody else, I should be happy to agree to that. But I am told that in the experience of the department cases are arising which make this a necessary measure.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I can understand cases
arising where a man has deliberately bonded his property by the issue of high interestbearing bonds and has taken the premium himself without putting it into his business. That, of course, is a form of fraud.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: He has a right to do it.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I do not say he is doing it illegally, but he is certainly doing it with the idea of defeating the act. A case of that kind should be met on its own merits in a different way. Now, money may at a given time be worth five per cent while a man is paying over 8 per cent for a period of say twenty years. If the minister will give me an assurance that the department will in a bona fide case allow the actual amount of interest paid, I shall not have another word to say, but there is no such assurance in the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: In the case cited by my hon. friend, where a man has paid 81 per cent; where that is the rate he is obliged to pay and he is going to pay it for twenty years, he should be allowed that rate. All these cases will have to be judged on their merits. In all laws of this kind somebody must have the responsibility and I do not know how you can do otherwise than leave it to the minister and trust him to exercise the power in a rational manner. As I say, though, if some other method could be devised it would be very agreeable to me.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Let us say that bonds
bearing interest at 6 per cent and extending over a term of five years are sold at 90; that would make the rate of interest 8 per cent. As I understand it, in a case like that the department will not allow the spread of that capital loss as an interest charge over the succeeding five years, though in the ordinary course of business that is exactly what is done. When a firm sells a bond issue at a loss they simply calculate it as an added interest on the bond, and in my opinion that is the way it should be dealt with by the department. But as I understand it, unless the matter is rectified in this legislation, the department simply call that a capital loss and no allowance is made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Does my hon. friend look upon that as fair treatment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: That is the law as it has been administered for some time. I am not anxious to invent troubles; I meet those that come. We were advised by the Department of Justice that the discount was a capital loss and should not be allowed.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Undoubtedly the Justice
department would give such a decision, based on the law as it stands, but what I suggest is that we should adjust the law so that what is in common practice recognized as an in-

Income Tax
terest charge shall be so regarded by the law. Then the Justice department would certainly give the opinion that under the amended law the discount would be an interest charge and not a capital loss.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Unless my memory is all wrong, these difficulties have arisen since I had anything to do with the administering of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Possibly.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I was not
familiar with that decision of the Justice department; I had thought that everybody was allowed his proper disbursements connected with the carrying on of his business. Certainly bank charges of interest, bank charges on a man's overdraft, on the discounting of his notes and so on, are very proper charges against his business, and I have never heard that challenged. Nor have I ever heard challenged what actually happens when a loan is made. Suppose money is worth 6 per cent and a business concern making a bond issue puts it out, for the purpose of keeping its credit in good shape, at 5 per cent, selling it at a discount. Now, when the investor buys bonds at a discount he regards it as just so much more interest to him, and if he buys it at a premium it is the same thing reversed. Unless firms are permitted to make that discount up in the ordinary added charges the effect is to make one rate of interest for the man who sells up to the market and another rate for the man who sells below the market, and that does not seem to be fair.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I assume that the department acting on the advice of the Justice department, has been following certain English decisions which may or may not be applicable to our act; at all events they think they are. Under these decisions the interest that has been paid to banks on what might be called current accounts, temporary loans, has been deducted, but interest payable in respect of bond issue has not been permitted to be deducted. These at all events are the English authorities, and I understand that the minister is introducing this legislation for the purpose of allowing a deduction on bond interest on other permanent securities. I am in sympathy with what the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) says, but at the same time I cannot shut my eyes to the fact that all over the country outrageous means are being resorted to for the purpose of evading the income tax. Those of us who are putting in honest statements, rendering an account up to the last cent of our income, are being penalized for our honesty in favour of people who are putting in statements that are not a bit better than a tissue of lies. I want to see something that will protect the honest man whose case was referred to by the hon. member for York-Sunbury but that will give the minister or will give someone the power, if a company makes a sham issue of bonds at an outrageous rate of interest, payable perhaps in New York or elsewhere outside the Dominion, and not taxable, to allow that business only the fair and legitimate amount of interest that ought to be borne by it. So far as this legislation is intended to prevent fraud of that character I am heartily in favour of it, but I would like to see the provision accompanied by some rider to protect the man who had honestly issued bonds at a high rate of interest some years ago from having to submit to a smaller rate of interest merely because the price of money drops for the moment. At the same time I wish to reaffirm my adhesion to the principle that the department or someone should have ample authority to prevent these outrageous frauds that are taking place in almost every direction.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I would like to ask a
question that is very much akin to some already asked, but it affects more particularly the man who borrows direct from the bank. When one borrows from a bank at 8 per cent the bank retains the interest at the time the loan is made. Suppose for instance one borrows $100 at 8 per cent, he will get only $92. The note is renewed every three months and the interest compounded would probably accumulate to almost 9 per cent. We will say 9 per cent for the purpose of illustrating the point. Would the borrower be allowed in connection with his income tax return the interest he has actually paid or just 8 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I doubt if you could
reduce these various suggestions into writing. You must allow some measure of discretion to someone, and I doubt if any better discretion can be exercised than the minister can bring to bear on the question. Temporary interest has hitherto been allowed. I would think in the case cited by my hon. friend that whatever is the usual and customary rate in that part of the country an intelligent minister would say should be allowed. We must suppose that the minister has some intelligence, and if in one part of the country the interest rate is a high one, if it is the ordinary current rate the minister would allow
449S
Income Tax

it, and if in other parts the interest rate is low, I think the minister ought to be allowed to recognize that as the proper rate. You must give some discretion to the minister whoever he may be. The suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John commends itself very much to me, but I doubt if you could put it into writing to make it effective. I can assure the House that there is no desire on the part of the minister to get any power in this matter, but I do not see how you can conduct a department of this character without having someone with some discretion to determine these matters in dispute. There is a ease I shall come to later where I am anxious to be relieved of authority. Far from seeking authority, I am trying to get rid of it.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
In connection with the
rate of interest to be added, and having in mind my hon. friend's illustration of a bond selling at 120, the minister takes power to determine what the rate shall be, but in the next clause in connection with discounts, that is of bonds sold at a discount, the minister does not take a similar power. Why should not the principle applicable in the one case be equally proper in the other? Why not take power in this act to determine whether the discount should be allowed as interest and not capital loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
This matter has been
settled in the practice of the department for some years, and I hesitate to depart from it. The department years ago ruled that the discount was a capital loss which should not be credited. I suppose something can be said on both sides of the question, but that has been the fixed policy of the department and I am reluctant to depart from it. In this matter I am rather disposed to take the doctrine "what we have we'll hold," and what we have not got we will try to get if it is necessary for efficient management.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Just one comment on the minister's explanation. Does he not see that the tendency is to drive issuing companies to issue at a high rate of interest so as to earn a premium rather than at a lower low rate of interest and sell at a discount? Just let me point out the advantages of a discount, if money happens temporarily to be dear. Very often a firm rather than fixing a high rate of interest on a long term bond would prefer to sell at a normal rate of interest and accept a discount spread over the term of the bond. That is preferable in my estimation in normal business to selling bonds at a high rate of interest and securing the

premium. The legislation presented here will have a tendency to force concerns to sell their bonds at a high rate of interest, which is certainly not in the interests of the department or the revenue of the country. I think while my hon. friend is certainly right in not seeking trouble, he must recognize that it is good business practice to sell a bond issue at a discount and absorb the loss in the interest charge from year to year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I have no doubt that a law like the Income Tax Act will at all times be open to suggestions of possible changes. I am inclined to think it is desirable that we should have a consolidation of the income tax law, and when we come to deal with that consolidation in a proper way these suggestions may well receive consideration. I would not like to adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend in this measure, which only aims to deal with a few points about which there ought not to be much difficulty.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I had a question which I wished to ask the minister more particularly with reference to clause 1. I will cite a concrete case to illustrate my point. I think the business income tax forms are called Form T and the agricultural forms Form TA. At all events that will serve for purposes of illustration. The case which I cite is that of an individual whose activities may be partly business and partly agricultural. In 1921 this individual made out his income tax returns on his two activities as a total but he was advised by one of the zone commissioners of taxation that that was improper, and that he would have to segregate the two. In segregating the two it was obligatory for him to take all his exemptions and place them against his agricultural tax bill, and use the other sum total of his business activities as a basis for taxation, upon which he paid the sum of $28 I believe. I think this year the same man is allowed to take the two activities together. I may say that if in 1921 he had been allowed to do that the sum payable would have been considerably less than $28, but I am not prepared to say exactly what it would be. I have wondered whether the returns sent in covering the year 1921 or the returns covering the year 1922 were correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
All I can say about that, if my hon. friend or anybody else is interested in a case and would be kind enough to send us a memorandum we would have it investigated. I would not like to answer offhand here. We get many applications and in most cases we are able to give satisfactory explanations.

Income Tax

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: When I am around my home many visitors come to ask me to assist them in making out their returns, and I usually abuse the tax form because of its complications. I have in mind a thought suggested by the statement made by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) that would be particularly applicable, in our rural municipalities in the western country where we keep a clerk upon full salary the year round paid out of municipal funds. Our provincial governments ask for an inventory each year, not for taxation purposes, but simply for the purpose of collecting data as to how much stock, how many horses, cattle, how much agricultural machinery and so forth each individual owns. This goes through the municipal clerk's hands, and I maintain that this inventory would be of assistance to the minister, if the municipal clerk was allowed say a very small percentage of the income tax that would be derived, I think it would be one of the best investments the minister could make. People do not send in wrong returns wilfully as is sometimes charged, but in many cases they are absolutely unable to make the returns out right. I am sure it would be a very good investment for the minister to adopt my suggestion, which I believe I made to the ex-Minister of Finance when he was occupying the position of minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I think it might be to the advantage of the committee if I proceeded to state the object of the several clauses and then perhaps it will not be necessary to go into the matter more in detail. Under the present law a foreign consul who is a citizen of a foreign country residing in Canada and devoting his whole time to diplomatic work is exempt from income tax, but that exemption does not apply to the officials of his staff. We propose that those officials shall also be exempt if they are citizens of a foreign country residing in Canada and devoting themselves entirely to diplomatic work, provided that a similar exemption is extended to Canadian officials in the country from which the foreign consul comes. This is reciprocity as respects not only the consul himself but also his staff.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Before the minister proceeds to section 5 would he give us a statement as to the necessity for section 3? I think he overlooked that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
The object of that, I
am informed, is that the expenses of each year shall be considered in connection with that year, but that each year must stand on its own bottom
Now, in the matter of pension exemptions. We exempt- pensions paid by the British or Canadian governments, but we do not exempt pensions paid by foreign governments. There are a number of citizens of Canada who have served in the armies of our allies and who have been aiiowed pensions. We propose to deal with them as we do those receiving pensions from the British or Canadian governments. The exemption, however, will apply only to those who served in the armies of our alllies during the war. That provision, I imagine, is not likely to be regarded with any objection.
Now in regard to the matter of penalties. I think much of the dissatisfaction with regard to the income tax-and I am aware that all tax laws must create dissatisfaction-results from the penalties which are imposed. The penalties that are imposed are of a substantial character, sometimes for very small offences. For example an employer fails to make a return as to those people in his employ as required by the act, and we impose penalties running up to as high as S50. We propose now to reduce that, and provide that the penalty shall not be less than $2 and shall not be more than $50, but it is to be governed by a percentage so that no more than 10 per cent of the amount of taxation would be paid in any case. The list of persons sent in in that way would be a list of persons paying only small sums, and we say the penalty for neglecting to send a return shall in any case be not more than 10 per cent of the taxation involved, with a further proviso that the penalty shall not be less than $2 or shall not be more than $50. In that way I hope we shall to a large extent meet the complaints that are made. The penalties undoubtedly seem to be severe for a small offence but I am hoping that in that respect there will be less complaint in future.
Now as to appeals. Under the present law provision is made for a board of appeal. I think I am correct in stating that neither in the time of my predecessor nor in my own has any one of these boards of appeal been created. The law is there and some people occasionally ask for an appeal. Experience has shown that by a little patience, correspondence, and negotiation we have generally managed to avoid the appeal and come to a settlement. However, I think there ought to be an appeal but not to the Minister of Finance. We hope, of course, that by continued correspondence, patient inquiry and good will we can avoid courts of appeal and come to a friendly settlement; but if in any case a
Income Tax

cantankerous person is not satisfied with the representations that are made and the judgment of the local officers, he ought to have the right of appeal but he had better not go to the Minister of Finance. We propose that he have the privilege of going to the Exchequer Court. These are the main, in fact the only, provisions of the bill.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I suppose we will have an opportunity of discussing section 7 of the resolution when the bill comes before us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
The bill will come up
in a moment or two and I would rather my hon. friend spoke now.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I should like to see that
section in the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Have you not a copy
of the bill?

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I have a copy of the bill here but it has not been introduced, therefore I avoided speaking on it. What I wish to point out to the minister is that section 25 of the bill carries out the intent of section 7 of the resolution creating a prior lien on all the assets, movable and immovable, of the taxpayer. Under the law as it exists at the present time there is a lien I know in favour of the government for any income tax owing. I think it may possibly be a prior lien but it is not a prior secured lien at the present time. Under the bill as drafted a prior lien will be created on all the assets of the individual. There is a proviso in this section that an individual may alienate personal property, but there is no provision that he may alienate his immovable property. In addition to this the minister might, perhaps, bear in mind that income tax is payable by instalments if need be. It would mean, I take it under this section of this bill that anybody intending to borrow, anybody desirous of effecting a mortgage on a piece of real estate, would first of all have to show the person from whom he was borrowing his receipt in full for his income tax before that person would lend him any money. If the tax-payer had paid his income tax in toto for the year there would be no difficulty; but if the taxpayer was paying it by instalments I question very much, in the event of his wanting to borrow, whether he would not be very seriously jeopardized by the provision of the clause as it is now drafted. I certainly would think that if he were mortgaging his property he would be. I suggest very respectfully to the minister that the clause as drafted is likely to create difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: There is a lien now, I believe but the effect of this is that the tax falls due, say, on 30th April, and the priority of lien takes effect from that moment. I shall have to give further thought to the suggestion of my hon. friend arising out of the payment of instalments. Of course we want the prior lien to be maintained and broadened if we can. We want to get our money; I am becoming a very mercenary person in all these matters.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I am quite aware there is a lien at the present time, and I think there is a prior lien. But this section of the bill as now drafted makes that lien an actual secured lien which is quite a different thing from an ordinary prior lien, and that is what I take exception to. Of course, if it is understood that way by the government, and the government does not think as I do that it would be a very serious matter for the borrowing public, I have nothing more to say. However, I think the point should be brought to the attention of the government. I might also say to the minister that this section will bear some discussion when the bill is brought down.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I have just one question I should like to ask and it is one in which many hundreds are interested. A short time ago I passed on to the minister a suggestion sent by a business man in the constituency from which I come. He was trying to find out if there was not some way to avoid the unnecessary trouble and expense to which many thousands are put to make out statements when they themselves know, and local authorities know, that their receipts only amount to a very small fraction of a taxable income. I know it is a difficult matter to adjust, but I can assure the minister if he can devise some way of saving that expense to those people he will confer a very great benefit upon them. It makes it necessary for most of them to go to a lawyer and have a statement made out, at an expense of from $2 to $5, and to a man who has lost Ins crop, or perhaps has had a very poor crop, that expense is quite an item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I have difficulty in understanding how he can obtain the knowledge without the return. I do not mind confessing that, when I was on the other side of the House and talked about this question, I expressed the pious hope that the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) would be able to do something to simplify this matter. The returns were very annoying.

Income Tax

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Much worse
than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I am free to confess that having had the responsibility on my own shoulders, I see great difficulty in attempting to simplify. What seemed to me an easy job is a very hard one. I do not see how you can gather the information, unless you lequire the return.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
The suggestion I passed to the minister from the business men was that a statement from the clerk of the municipality-and I think I might add also, on my own behalf, a statement from the banker 

should surely be sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: We want uniformity of practice. We cannot oblige the municipal clerk or the banker to make the return. I wish I could make it simpler. I know it is a worry. When I have to make up my own return I get very "mad."

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: The minister will remember when we were discussing the act last year I drew to his attention that I, during the latter term of my office, had heard that companies were being incorporated for the purpose of enabling them to avoid taxes. I was surprised the other day to have a gentleman dealing in rather a large way, come to me-he thought I was in business-with a view of getting an incorporation of a private holding company which would enable him to defeat the purposes of the income tax. I drew the matter to my hon. friend's attention last year, and he said he would look into it and follow it up. I have been told since that it has become a common practice. My hon. friend will very easily find lots of people within a very short distance who would do it. I would like to know the minister's idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I am afraid there is too much foundation for what the hon. member has mentioned. We are giving the matter some attention, and if we are fortunate enough to be able to complete before next session the consolidation which I referred to, I think we will have to deal with the matter very seriously. For the moment we are not able to deal with it. I regret to say that reports have reached me that there is too much foundation for what my hon. friend has said.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I am glad to see the minister has arrived at that conclusion. He will find that reports that have reached him have not been exaggerated.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: It would require only a very short section of the act. Could protection not be put in now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: It is a difficult matter to deal with.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I desire to bring to the attention of the minister a case which seems to me to be one of gross unfairness, where a tax is not levied on a man's net income. An acquaintance of mine, a farmer, met with crop failure for two seasons. Being a veterinary surgeon, he went out to make his living at his former profession. He made a little money, and had to pay income tax on it. His money all went to clear his debt on his location; and at the end of the year there was nothing left even to pay the income tax. It was a gross hardship to pay any tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I think the new section will cover the case. Where a man is engaged in two occupations difficulties arise, but under this section power will be vested in the minister to determine what is his chief occupation and on that he must pay.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: But that is a tax on a man's net income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: No, that is too broad a statement. He might make $20,000 in a year, which is subject to taxation; he might go out and speculate, lose it all, and have no income, and he would have no tax to pay. That is an extravagant illustration, but it is based on what has occurred. That which is his greatest income should be taxed. We cannot prevent a man speculating, but we do not want the income tax to suffer on that account.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Does the minister think it is necessary to adopt paragraph No. 8 of the resolution, which says:
8. That when the minister has knowledge or suspects that any person is or is about to become indebted to a tax-payer he may demand of such person that the moneys otherwise payable to the tax-payer be in whole or in part paid over to the Receiver General of Canada on account of the tax-payer's liability under this act.
We already find the minister under paragraph 7 stating that all taxes, interest and penalty payable under the act shall constitute a lien upon the assets of the taxpayers both real and personal, a condition that does not exist in reference to municipal or provincial taxation. But has he a right to go out on a roving hunting commission, whenever or wherever he suspects a man to have any dealings with the taxpayer, and register a letter and send it to that man, and say "Do not pay that man what you owe him; pay it all to me?" I do not think, with all the other means they have of collecting, it is necessary to give the minister such extreme powers as those.
Income Tax

Is there any precedent in any other country where a man can make use of a mere suspicion and go out and take action of that kind? I object to the word "suspect." If he only has a mere suspicion, he can hold up this man and prevent the payment of money to him that would perhaps really be of substantial benefit to him at the moment. Meanwhile, while the consideration of the adjustment of his taxation goes on, which might last for two or three months, the money is withheld from him and he cannot make use of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I am told there is a
precedent in the United States law, but that is not the best reason in the world. However, I am advised in the light of experience that something of this kind is necessary. All sorts of attempts are made to evade taxation, and we must have privileges in the method of guarding the revenue which in view of some people are not necessary. We ought to have the benefit of the doubt in the matter of saving the revenue. We all have a common interest in that.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Does the minister think the ordinary garnishee process is not sufficient? I rather think this is an extraordinarily wide power, and if arbitrarily operated it might work a very great injustice. I hate to see a power like this placed in the hands of the tax collector of any government, I do not care what the personnel might be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Least of all, I do not think hon. members need fear that any power we have- will be exercised in an arbitrary spirit. The manner in which the income tax has been applied by my predecessor and in my own day would indicate that there was no desire to use the power arbitrarily. I think every desire is manifested to make it as easy as possible. A few cases will arise under this provision, and if they arise, I think hon. members will not object to our exercising the power given to us.
Resolution reported.
On the motion for the second reading of
the resolution:

speechtext: I wish to say-
