speechtext:
Under rule 17 A this motion is not debatable. Later on the hon. member will have an opportunity to speak.
Motion agreed to and resolution read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Fielding thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 249 to amend The Income War Tax Act, 1917.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. FIELDING moved the second reading of the bill.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I must confess that I was keenly disappointed on reading this bill. I was disappointed at the fact that there was no provision, in the matter of earned and unearned income, no provision regarding exemption on account of children, and no provision with reference to persons married under the regime of community of property. No one realizes more than I do the tremendous task of the Minister of Finance; no one appreciates to a greater extent than I do his earnestness, his ability and knows the many demands that are made upon him. But surely when these demands are reasonable, when they are in the public interest, the minister should yield to some of them, to some extent at least. In this special instance I venture to say, from the discussion which arose on this question when it was brought up on a previous occasion, that it was the wish of this parliament that some amendment should be introduced regarding the proposal which was put before the House. When I submitted my resolution on March 21st touching these matters, it was passed unanimously; there was not one dissenting voice raised against it. On the 17th of May, when I renewed my proposal, I think it was evident that I had the sympathy of the whole House in the matter. There was not a single word of opposition. I am fully aware that in order to meet our obligations we must get as much revenue as we can. But I submit that we should get that revenue from the people who are most able to pay. I will not weary the House with the arguments that I have already advanced. I am sure that the minister is himself convinced of the soundness of my proposals, and he must have had very good reasons for not bringing in the amendments suggested. It is not asking too much, I hope, to request an explanation from the minister of the reasons why he did not incorporate these amendments into the bill. I feel confident that were I to submit an amendment to the House it would carry. But I will refrain from doing so until the Minister of Finance explains why these amendments were not included in the bill. I do not say that when the bill is before the committee I will not propose them. However, I shall listen to the reasons the minister may offer and I hope that before the bill reaches that stage he will give to the House some satisfactory reasons for not bringing forward the amendments and at the same time assure us that in the near future legislation will be enacted to provide

Income Tax
for the readjustment of income taxation more in line with justice and equity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: I wish I were as free as my hon. friend to advocate all these popular notions, because they are popular, I am sure. But I regret to say that I am not, because I must have regard to the condition of the revenue. The hon. gentleman brought forward his motion last year and we took it into consideration. More than that, we made some concession. That, I think, should be evidence that I am not so absolutely unyielding as he pictures me. As to a larger review of the Income Tax Act, if it is necessary, I hope that my hon. friend will have patience enough to wait for that consolidation which, without giving any guarantee, I trust will be undertaken in time for next session. I am sorry that I cannot give any reasons that will be satisfactory to my hon. friend because I know how zealous and enthusiastic he is in the matter. But we cannot have everything we want in this wicked world; we must wait patiently for some of the things we much desire.

maintopic: THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT, 1917, AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
As I understand from the minister that next year there is likely to be a consolidation of the act I will in no way suggest to him any amendments I might have to submit to the bill he is now bringing down. On the other hand it is more than probable that no opportunity will be afforded myself or any other hon. member to study the proposed consolidation before it is brought down next year. It will therefore be as well for me now to suggest to the minister certain matters which I should like him to take into consideration when he does undertake the consolidation he has announced.
The first point I want him to consider in that consolidation is the question to which I referred previously this evening, as to the payment on net income of the taxpayer. Where the taxpayer has legal deductions under class B income, if those deductions exceed the total of his class B income, then I think he should be permitted to have a deduction for the surplus made from class A income. In short, the taxpayer should pay on his net income. There is another point which I would draw to the attention of the minister and that is in regard to the manner in which the tax is computed at present. There is the normal tax, there is the surtax, and there is the interest on the
11 pan. surtax or the supertax. This is not only exceedingly onerous on

those who are unfortunate enough to have to pay income tax, but it makes it very difficult indeed to compute the tax. Another question that comes to my mind, and which possibly may not be very popular in this House or to the minister but which I would venture to suggest nevertheless, even at this time of the session. I believe that the income tax to-day is far too heavy. That tax under the act as it stands at present is not helping to stimulate savings; it is not stimulating business. I believe that the taxpayers, having to pay as they do pay to-day very heavy taxes, are utterly unable to invest any money in industrial concerns, and for that reason the progress of the country is seriously impeded. In the United States, if I might refer to that republic for a moment, a deduction is allowed, or a lesser tax is levied on account of the savings of a particular taxpayer. If a taxpayer can show a bona fide saving in any year, he is allowed a lesser rate of taxation on the amount actually saved. This encourages economy, which is very essential in this country and I think it is a very important question that should receive careful consideration when the minister comes to take up the consolidation that he has mentioned. Certain deductions are allowed under the present income tax law. Under the act as passed in 1917-this was during the war of course-deductions were allowed for contributions made to the Red Cross and patriotic funds. I am aware, as I think are other members also, that representations have been made to the minister to allow deductions for contributions to bona fide charitable or educational institutions. The deductions allowed under the 1917 act for contributions to the Red Cross and patriotic funds were subsequently withdrawn. The work which those funds carry on is far from finished, and there are numerous charities badly in need of funds not only in the city of Montreal but all over the country. These charities are having greater difficulty year by year in securing funds for carrying on their work, which, in part at least, is really the duty of the state. I ask that contributions made to bona fide charitable and educational institutions be allowed as deductions, or that they be taken into consideration when the new act is framed.
It is quite true that the minister will immediately say: Well, all these demands must mean a diminution in the revenue. I quite admit that, but still as regards charitable and educational institutions I do not think the state can claim for one moment that deductions allowed for contributions to them will

Income Tax
not eventually enure ten times more to the benefit of the state. Again I quote the income tax law of the United States, under which individual tax-payers-not corporations -are allowed deductions up to 15 per cent of their taxable income, provided that these deductions are paid to a charitable or educational institution approved of in the proper way. There is no question that in allowing deductions of this description and allowing also a taxpayer to pay on his net income alone-which do seem to me perfectly fair and reasonable requests to make-there will be a certain reduction in the amount which will be collected under the income tax law. On the other hand, possibly it is pertinent to suggest that the income tax law was originally framed for the purpose of paying our war debt. Whether the amount derived from income tax can ever be segregated for this purpose I cannot presume to say, but I think I may go this far, that the time does seem to have arrived when the people are strained to the uttermost in their efforts to pay taxes. I am perfectly aware that without these taxes the budget cannot be made to balance as we are budgetting at the present time. The only suggestion I venture to make in these last days of the session is that we should really live within our income, and that our budgets should, if possible, be made to balance with the taxes that are collected. It is quite true that my suggestions would mean a certain decrease in the net revenue collected from income tax, but at the same time it would be an encouragement to people to be charitable and economical.
It seems to me that with our budget deficits year by year we must come to the point sooner or later, and the sooner the better, when we should live strictly within our income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How?

By spending less, by actually cutting out many, many things we now spend money on. Perhaps this is the most unpopular thing for any member to say in the dying days of the session, and I suppose everyone will criticize me.
Not at all.

But let our expenditure be pared down ruthlessly. We should reduce our expenditure to the very minimum and restrict it to keeping our buildings and our public works in repair, in order that we may make our budgets balance without having to increase taxation.

I have been
greatly cheered to hear the remarks of the

hon. gentleman. We have heard speeches along exactly the same lines from this side of the House. We have deplored the increases both of taxation and of expenditure. We now find all our work has not been in vain, and we look fonvard to the early date when my hon. friend will cross over here-not to take a place down in the comer, but to take his seat among us and really do something to try to cut down expenditure. We are assured that so far as he is concerned none of these extra supplements were brought down until the thirteenth hour passed.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Income to be not less than income from chief occupation.

Observing as I do that we are now almost through with the second budget of this government, and that it has left the income tax schedules in the same condition as it found them, and remembering also the aspirations-to use the most euphemistic term I can think of-of hon. gentlemen opposite and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) himself, may I inquire if after eighteen months he has not been able to invade the precincts of the profiteer and ease the burden on the masses? And does he hope by remodelling and changing the schedules at some later and undefined time to achieve this end? How is it we have had to wait eighteen months to get the burden on the masses eased and the profiteer brought to book? Is the progress of the future to be as slow as the progress of the past? Is there really any room left for hope?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not heard any
allegations that anybody is engaged in profiteering. I had understood that the profiteering was usually carried on during the regime of my right hon. friend. Eighteen months, you know, is a short period in the life of a nation. We are not going to accomplish immediately all that he mentions, but I hope that as years roll on, with patience and courtesy and good will all round, some of these results will be brought about in the natural order of things. I suggest that my right hon. friends be patient and that they rather bear those ills they have than fly to others that they know not of.

I quite realize the solemn truth and wisdom of the Finance Minister's assertion that anything we may hope for will come in the natural order; it certainly will not come in the government order, we may be quite certain of that. Then, he advises the

Income Tax
country to bear the ills they have rather than fly to others they know not of. Well, the country is already impressed with the necessity for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I gave the advice to my hon. friends, not to the country.

I also am, as the whole country is, thoroughly imbued with that truth, and I think the people are very regretful-the evidences of it are not a few-that they had not been imbued with it and acted upon it sooner. Yes, I admit that times were better in our day; profits were greater on the part of all classes of the country-I am compelled to admit it. We, however, enacted certain legislation to take for the nation a share of those profits, and we were assailed because we did not take more from the profiteer and less from the masses. Now I wonder how it is that in this session we are amending the very bill that apportions as between the profiteer and the masses, and still the Finance Minister can scarcely dot an i or cross a t.

Section agreed to.
On section 7, subsection 15-Notice of dissatisfaction respecting the decision of the minister.

That seems unfair and improper. If a man has a case that the minister himself thinks ought to be considered by the court, I do not know why as a preliminary to his going to the court he must put up security for costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The suggestion came from a very well informed source that that is a wise precaution. It has been well considered and I am confident that it will serve a good purpose.
I see it is entirely satisfactory to the minister; I hope he will assure us that no litigant who has the right under the act to go to the court will be denied that right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend can be
assured that the good spirit in which this act has always been administered will be continued.
Subsection 15 of section 7 agreed to.
On section 10-Taxes to be a lien.

That is the section to
which I had reference a moment ago. It creates on the property movable and immovable of every taxpayer a prior lien ranking before any other obligation of any description. In addition to that, the section
287i
as drafted is retroactive from the first of January, 1923. It means that any creditor lending to a debtor on any security, whether it is personal property or real property, will first have to satisfy himself whether or not the taxpayer's income tax has been fully paid I can say positively that no person would lend on mortgage in the province of Quebec without first satisfying himself that the income tax had been totally paid under this section. Moreover, the section allows the transfer of personal property to a bona fide purchaser but it allows no transfer of immovable property. The section is an exceedingly dangerous one. I do not complain in the least degree of the power it puts in the hands of the government, but I do complain of the difficulties it will put in the way of very many borrowers. The government should content itself with a prior unsecured lien, not with a prior secured lien on the property of the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend states it, we want a secured lien if we can get it. I realize there is something in what my hon. friend says, but I wish he would not press his suggestion now. It will be a short time, after all, before this matter can be reviewed again, and if experience shows that the trouble my hon. friend suggests has arisen we can deal with it in the consolidation. I am hoping the trouble will not be as serious as he suggests.

There is not the slightest shadow of a doubt that the trouble will actually be there when this legislation goes into effect. I am not pressing anything on the minister; I am only explaining the exact effect this legislation will have on the borrowing public, particularly as affecting mortgages in the province of Quebec. If the minister wishes to press the section, of course I will do nothing else but agree to it, but I suggest the insertion after the word "personal" in line 19, of the words "and real"-in other words, differentiating between personal and immovable property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
read the clause as he suggests it be amended?

The proviso reads:
Provided always, however, that the lien or charge hereby created shall not follow or attach to personal property.
I suggest inserting here the words " or real " before " property."

That would discharge the lien entirely.
Income Tax

No. The effect would be that the purchaser would not have to follow whether or not the income tax had been paid. Without this proviso you could not purchase a stock or a bond or a piece of real estate without first inquiring whether this lien, which is an actual mortgage on the man's property, has been fully paid.
It is simply a case of another search of taxes.

Yes, but this tax may
extend over a term of months. Are we going to insist on the taxpayer paying his whole tax at once before he can sell his stock, before he can sell a bond or a piece of real estate? It is unreasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it has the effect of inducing the taxpayer to pay up, that at least is one of the virtues. I hope my hon. friend will find that the evil is not so serious as he suggests. When we come to the consolidation possibly we may be able to meet his views.

Might I suggest to the minister an amendment, to add after the word "personal" in the nineteenth line "or immovable." That does not affect the intention of the section in the very least because it intends to allow a bona fide seller to sell to a bona fide purchaser his personal property. I only want to make it clear that a bona fide seller may sell to a like purchaser his immovable property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend
will not press it.
I dislike pressing my hon. friend, but what reason is there why it should not be included? I think I am entitled to at least get an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
cress I will delay the third reading and give the matter consideration but at this stage I think we might accept the section as it is.
I would like to ask whether the opinion of the Department of Justice has been taken as to the power of this parliament to enact section 7.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that the
Department of Justice has so advised.

With all respect I would
like to differ from the department, and I do not think anyone would have much to fear about that. While parliament has the power to enforce, that must be within reasonable limits, and to say merely because it is a Crown debt it thereby operates as a lien on real and personal property goes far beyond 
any express or implied power of the Dominion parliament. A Crown debt takes priority and always will take priority in the administration of assets over other creditors, but that this parliament can legislate so as to constitute a debt due the federal Crown a mortgage upon any particular piece of property in the province I shall always doubt until it is resolved by some authority even higher than the Department of Justice.
I think this section purports to create such a mortgage.

Section agreed to.
On section 26-Collection of tax from third party.
Will the minister give us an explanation of this? It seems a rather unusual section. It says, "When the minister has knowledge or suspects that any person" and so forth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told that this
arises from actual events coming under the observation of the department. This is really necessary to prevent evasions of the law. The cases arising would not be numerous, but I think it will be a preventive measure in a large degree. There is a tendency in many lines for people to evade this income tax law. It is almost as open to evasion as the customs law when crossing the border, but all these changes are the result of experience in the department, I am assured. The cases are not likely to occur very often, but they will occur occasionally and I think the existence of a clause like this will help to prevent fraud.

Section agreed to.
On section 28-Certificate of default to be registered as judgment.

Has the minister done
anything towards preventing what is really the grossest system of evasion possible? That is to say, the formation of what are really personal companies to which are assigned the assets of an individual and out of which the individual draws an amount that is really not his income at all but merely the sum he lives on, allowing the rest to accumulate and thereby escape all the income tax except the corporation tax alone. I wonder if the minister has done anything to meet that situation which has arisen practically wholly in his own time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman who sits behind my hon. friend raised that question in his absence and we had a little discussion

Income Tax
on it. I cannot say that anything particular has been clone. I realize that there is too much ground for the view that the law is being evaded. The matter is engaging our attention, and if the consolidation is brought about which we hope, it ought to be included. At the moment we are not sufficiently well advised to deal with it. I quite realize that there is something along the lines suggested by the right hon. gentleman.

It is far more important than consolidation. It is a matter of millions upon millions. Other countries have met it, and why has this government spent eighteen months during which this evasion has been rampant and taken no step even to copy the legislation of other countries? It is a gross indictment of the administration, I may impress upon the minister.
Does my hon. friend mean to suggest that these so-called companies have been incorporated since the present administration came into office?
Practically all.
Surely my hon. friend is not serious when he suggests that.
There may have been some incorporations taken place before. The income tax has not been in force for so many years, but the effect in the way of evading the tax has been since that time.
No.

If the hon. member knew before I wonder he has not impressed it on the government and tried to get some remedy before this. He apparently knew before 1921. Why has he not brought that to the attention of the minister?
How does my right hon. friend know I have not impressed it on the government ?

If he has, it has been rather an ineffective pressure. If the hon. member for the St. Lawrence-St. George division of Montreal (Mr. Marler) has no more effect on the government than to keep on pressing eighteen months and get nothing, it seems to me that it might be a good suggestion for him to go back to his constituents. He comes from a portion of Canada from which he ought to be able to speak with authority. Surely he can produce something more than pious aspirations from the lips of the Minister of Finance.

That is precisely the reason I spoke the way I did to my hon. friend,
because I thought I did speak with some authority. This act has been in force since the 20th of September, 1917. My hon. friend comes forward to-night and charges that most of these companies have been brought into effect since this government came into power.
The evasions have.

My hon. friend has been so very kind in his remarks to me that perhaps he will allow me to continue. Companies were brought into existence during the administration of my right hon. friend. Did he take any action?

My hon. friend has asked a question? Now perhaps he will permit mo to answer. He must remember that the income tax refers to the year previous and previous to a certain date in that year, and as a consequence the incorporation of the company would require to be about the year 1918 or 1919 to have any effect at all so far as our income tax collection was concerned.
I never heard of such an incorporation myself within those years I want to tell my hon. friend, until virtually before we went out of office.
I am prepared to accept the hon. gentleman's word but not his assertion that this government has not done as much as his government.

They had reason to do a whole lot more because the effect of the evasions has been since we went out of office. The hon. member knows that. The loss to the revenue has been in the last two years. The effect certainly has been recently even of incorporations in 1918, which would be the first year they were incorporated.
I am sorry to differ.
Of course it has been. Does he mean to say it has not been in these last two years?
It has not been wholly in these two years. That is the assertion I made at the commencement.

At all events it has been very nearly wholly, and you cannot get thing? cured just in a minute. The last time we were in office was in the year 1920-21, and I do not think that evasion had effect up to that time. It has only had effect since then
Nothing but righteousness happened up to that time!

Mostly so, or punished crime. But now we find, it seems to me

in the words of John Hay, "Nothing but unpitied suffering and unpunished crime.-'

Section agreed to.
On section 11-Act to come into force.
May I make another plea to the Minister of Finance?
Hear, hear.

To suggest that section 25 of the act shall not go into effect until the commencement of the 1924 period of taxation. There is to be a consolidation of the act next year. I am only asking that this particular section 25 be delayed for a year. Six months of the year have already elapsed.

On section 4-Security for advances.
May I ask the minister if the harbour commissioners are regularly paying the interest charges on the loans that have so far been made to them?
Yes, every cent of interest has been paid. Last year they paid in interest the sum of $1,138,062.12. They also paid the amount necessary for a sinking fund, and had a surplus of over S200,000.

Section agreed to.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Lapointe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 250, to provide for further advances to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Mr. LAPOINTE moved the second reading of the bill.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
On section 2-an additional $10,000,000 may be advanced to the corporation for the construction of terminal facilities.

This bill has
not been distributed. Is it in the usual form?

It is exactly in the form of the preceding bill-word for word.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of and concurrence in the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 83, respecting banks and banking.

Bank Act

What is the nature of the
amendments made to this bill by the Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think most of the
amendments are of an unimportant character. One of the amendments relates to the question of insurance. There was much discussion in the Banking and Commerce committee, and a clause was put in the act preventing any bank agent from acting as representative of an insurance company. That is the substance of it. An amendment has been made which is designed to meet the case of the Weyburn bank. It was represented in the Senate that the agent of that bank received a considerable portion of his income from the handling of hail insurance, and if that were taken from him, it would practically destroy his income. I have no personal knowledge of this, but I understand that representations made to the Senate led them to adopt words which would practically have the effect I have stated, although they did not mention the name of that bank. The amendment proposed by the senate reads:
After subclause 3 of clause 76 insert the following as subclause 4:
"4. Nothing herein contained shall prevent the agent or manager of a bank, with chief office and branches in one province only, from acting as agent for the placing of hail insurance."
There is no mention made of the Weyburn bank, but I understand it is to meet that particular case. There is one amendment regarding the issue of stock not below par. That is technical, and there is no objection to it.
On page 45 of the bill, section 88, a clause was inserted by the Banking and Commerce committee protecting the unpaid vendor in certain cases. That clause has been stricken out by the Senate.
I do not concur in that amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In section 91 the language in the clause relating to discount says:
The rate of interest or discount charged by the bank shall appear on the face of the note.
These words were struck out by the Senate. I think these are the most material alterations. The rest are purely technical as far as I remember.

I desire to protest against the elimination of the protection for the unpaid vendor under section 88. I have no desire to delay the House at all. I think it is important that that clause should remain.

I have no objection to the amendment regarding insurance, nor yet have I any material objection to the amendment
to section 88; but I have a serious objection to the amendment proposed to section 91. I think the rate of interest or discount should appear in every case on the face of the note.
I understood, while in the committee, that the bankers themselves had no objection to this provision, and I cannot understand what interest would be in any way jeopardized by having the rate of interest appear as the Banking and Commerce committee desired.
1 would, therefore, oppose the Senate amendment to section 91.
Why?
Why should it? Why should the dealings between one man and the bank be disclosed to another party? I do not think there is any serious objection to the amendment.

In order to meet the situation my hon. friend suggests, why not exclude drafts from the operation of the section? The section, as I understand it, was designed as a deterrent to banks in charging an excess rate of interest.

You cannot
differentiate between a draft and a promissory note. If the objection is valid against one it is against the other. But I have never been able to see what purpose was served by having the rate of interest or the discount appear on the note. There might have been reasons given but unfortunately I was not present when the committee dealt with this clause.
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.
Dairy Industry Act

Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of bill No. 241 to amend the Dairy Industry Act 1914.
Motion agreed to bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Definition.

There is a slight omission in the bill as printed. I move that a new section 1 be added as follows:
Paragraph (k) of section 3 of the Dairy Industry Act, 1914, chapter 7, of the statutes of 1914, is amended by striking out the word "or", in the second last line thereof, and substituting the word "and" therefor.

Amendment agreed to.
On section 2 (new section 3)-Minimum standard of fat in butter.

Paragraph
(d) provides that no person shall manufacture, import into Canada, or sell any milk or cream which contains any fat or oil other than that of milk. Would it not make it more clear if, after the word "cream',, the words "or substitute therefor" were inserted?
It would do no harm if my hon. friend wants to make assurance doubly sure.

I move that the section be amended accordingly.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 5-Establishment of guilt for violation of act.

There may be some stocks of filled milk or filled cream on hand by some dealers and it was thought advisable that the section relating thereto might not come into force until the dealers have had time to get rid of those stocks. I therefore move that there be added to the bill as section 7 the following provision:
Section 3 (original section 2) of this act shall not come into effect until October 1st, 1923.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
